parts.text: Jhang Dyeing Mills is a dyeing and finishing mill near Faisalabad that uses large amounts of water and gas. Analyse two ways Jhang Dyeing Mills could make its operations more sustainable.
parts.answer: 1. Water recycling: installing a treatment plant to reuse dyeing water reduces the amount drawn from falling groundwater and stops untreated discharge into canals; this lowers water costs and fines and helps meet European buyers' sustainability requirements, protecting export orders. 2. Energy efficiency: heat recovery from boilers and solar panels reduce gas use; costs fall as gas prices rise and CO₂ emissions per metre fall, improving competitiveness and reputation. Investment costs and payback must be considered.
parts.working: Ways: water treatment/reuse, renewable energy, efficient machinery, waste reduction, lean production, sustainable materials. Mark scheme: AO1 knowledge 2, AO2 application 2, AO3 analysis 4. Level 2 (5–8): two developed chains of analysis, each clearly applied to this business. Level 1 (1–4): knowledge and/or application with undeveloped or generic analysis. Evaluation earns no extra marks.

stem: Indigo Denim produced 1.2 million metres of denim in 2023 using 180 million litres of water. In 2025, after introducing new washing machines, it produced 1.6 million metres using 176 million litres of water.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage reduction in water used per metre of fabric between 2023 and 2025. Give your answer to 1 decimal place.
parts.working: 2023: 180 million ÷ 1.2 million = 150 litres per metre (M1). 2025: 176 million ÷ 1.6 million = 110 litres per metre (M1). Reduction = (150 − 110) ÷ 150 × 100 = 26.7 % (A1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one reason why improving efficiency in this way could help Indigo Denim's operations strategy.
parts.answer: Lower water use per metre reduces costs and dependence on a scarce resource, so Indigo Denim can keep producing even if water supply is restricted and can show buyers measurable sustainability improvements, supporting a strategy of competing on quality and responsible production.
parts.working: 1 mark for knowledge of the term/concept; up to 2 marks for explaining it in the context of the business (application).

author: HomiLabs

stem:
WoodWorks makes furniture in Chiniot. Timeline:
2020: Job production of custom furniture for households. Revenue Rs 400 million; average lead time 6 weeks.
2021: Changes to batch production of standard designs. Unit costs fall 18 %; lead time 3 weeks.
2022: Wins contracts to furnish 12 new hotels. Custom household orders fall by half.
2023: Buys CNC cutting machines (Rs 150 million). Capacity doubles. Revenue Rs 720 million.
2024: Switches to cheaper imported wood. Customer returns rise from 2 % to 6 %.
2025: Hotel construction slows. Capacity utilisation 62 %.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate the effectiveness of WoodWorks' operations strategy between 2020 and 2025.
parts.answer: Effective: switching from job to batch production in 2021 cut unit costs by 18 % and lead times from 6 to 3 weeks, helping the move into hotel contracts; the 2023 CNC machines increased capacity and consistency of quality, and revenue grew from Rs 400m to Rs 720m. Less effective: the move to batch production reduced flexibility — custom orders fell and some loyal household customers left; the 2024 decision to import cheaper wood led to quality complaints (returns rose to 6 %) and reputational damage; capacity utilisation fell to 62 % in 2025 after the large investment as hotel construction slowed. Judgement: the strategy was effective for growth and cost reduction up to 2023, but less so afterwards because it relied heavily on one market (hotels) and compromised quality; overall partially effective — it must rebalance flexibility and quality. Consider external factors (economy, construction slowdown) separately from strategy.
parts.working: Use the timeline: production method change, automation, sourcing decision, capacity, quality data. Criteria: cost, quality, flexibility, capacity utilisation, revenue. Judgement. Levels: Level 4 (16–20): accurate knowledge, strong use of the case data, three or four developed chains of analysis and a well-supported judgement/recommendation throughout, specific to this business and its situation. Level 3 (11–15): developed analysis in context with some supported evaluation. Level 2 (6–10): some analysis, mostly descriptive use of the case; evaluation weak or unsupported. Level 1 (1–5): knowledge with little application.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Punjab Foods (an invented company) makes packaged snacks and frozen foods. Appendix 1: energy is 20 % of production costs; electricity prices rose 40 % in two years. Appendix 2: sales of standard snacks are flat; demand for 'healthy' snacks is growing 12 % a year. Appendix 3: a major supermarket chain and two export customers will require suppliers to cut carbon emissions by 30 % by 2030. Appendix 4: the main plant runs at 92 % capacity utilisation; gearing is 48 %.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Advise the directors of Punjab Foods on its operations strategy for the next five years.
parts.answer: Options: (1) Cost focus: expand the main plant, automate packing, centralise production for economies of scale — supports price competition with rivals, but large investment and less flexibility. (2) Sustainability focus: solar power (energy is 20 % of costs and electricity prices rising), reduce packaging waste, source from local farmers — lowers long-run costs, meets supermarket and export buyers' requirements (Appendix 3), improves brand; higher upfront costs. (3) Flexibility/innovation: smaller batch lines for new healthy products (demand growing 12 % a year). Recommendation: combine sustainability investments with a clear payback (solar, waste reduction) and flexible lines for the growing healthy segment, rather than pure scale expansion; justify with appendix data on energy costs, buyer requirements and demand; phase investment given finance constraints; set KPIs (cost per unit, energy per tonne, waste).
parts.working: Use appendices; weigh cost, quality, flexibility, sustainability and finance; clear recommendation. Levels: Level 4 (16–20): accurate knowledge, strong use of the case data, three or four developed chains of analysis and a well-supported judgement/recommendation throughout, specific to this business and its situation. Level 3 (11–15): developed analysis in context with some supported evaluation. Level 2 (6–10): some analysis, mostly descriptive use of the case; evaluation weak or unsupported. Level 1 (1–5): knowledge with little application.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define the term 'quality assurance'.
parts.answer: A system of setting agreed quality standards at every stage of production and checking that they are met, so that errors are prevented rather than detected at the end; often each worker is responsible for quality.
parts.working: 1 mark: standards set for each stage / process; 1 mark: prevent defects / all workers responsible.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one difference between quality control and quality assurance for a medicine manufacturer.
parts.answer: Quality control inspects finished tablets at the end of the line and rejects faulty batches (detecting errors), whereas quality assurance builds checks into every stage — raw materials, mixing, pressing — so faults are prevented; QA should reduce costly wasted batches.
parts.working: 1 mark each: QC = inspection/detect at end; QA = prevent at every stage; 1 mark: application.

stem: Hashmi Ceramics makes dinner plates. In 2024 it made 74,000 plates and 1,850 were rejected. In 2025, after introducing kaizen groups, it made 80,000 plates and its reject rate fell to 0.9 %.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the reject rate at Hashmi Ceramics in 2024.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the number of plates rejected in 2025.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain the term 'kaizen' and how it may have helped Hashmi Ceramics.
parts.answer: Kaizen means continuous improvement through many small changes suggested by workers. Production teams at Hashmi may have suggested small changes, e.g. adjusting kiln temperatures or handling methods, which together cut the reject rate from 2.5 % to 0.9 %.
parts.working: 1 mark: continuous small improvements; 1 mark: workers involved/teams; 1 mark: application to reject rate.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: RestWell Inns, a chain of 14 budget hotels, is considering introducing total quality management (TQM). Analyse two benefits of TQM for RestWell Inns.
parts.answer: 1. Consistent service quality: TQM makes every employee — receptionists, cleaners, cooks — responsible for quality and focused on internal and external customers; fewer mistakes (dirty rooms, wrong bills) mean better online reviews and repeat bookings, raising occupancy. 2. Lower costs: getting things right first time reduces the cost of complaints, refunds and re-cleaning rooms; staff empowerment and teamwork may improve motivation, reducing labour turnover in a high-turnover industry.
parts.working: Benefits: quality culture, customer satisfaction/reviews, lower cost of errors, motivation/empowerment, competitive advantage. Mark scheme: AO1 knowledge 2, AO2 application 2, AO3 analysis 4. Level 2 (5–8): two developed chains of analysis, each clearly applied to this business. Level 1 (1–4): knowledge and/or application with undeveloped or generic analysis. Evaluation earns no extra marks.

stem: StepUp Shoes makes leather shoes in Lahore. It holds 5 weeks of materials, wastes 8 % of the leather it buys, and makes large batches of each design. Workers are paid piece rates and supervised closely. Cheaper imported shoes have taken 15 % of its market over three years.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate whether introducing lean production would improve the competitiveness of StepUp Shoes.
parts.answer: For: lean techniques (JIT, kaizen, cell production, waste reduction) could cut the 5 weeks of materials inventory and 8 % waste of leather, lowering costs so StepUp can compete with cheaper imports; cell production and multi-skilled teams increase flexibility to produce smaller batches of new designs quickly, important as fashions change; quality improves. Against: lean needs reliable suppliers (if leather comes from small tanneries with variable quality, JIT deliveries could stop production), investment in training and a change in culture from the current piece-rate, supervisor-led system; workers may resist; benefits take time. Judgement: lean production would improve competitiveness, especially through waste reduction and flexibility, if introduced gradually with training and supplier development; full JIT is risky until supply is reliable.
parts.working: Lean elements; costs, quality, flexibility; preconditions (suppliers, culture, training); judgement. Mark scheme: AO1 knowledge 2, AO2 application 2, AO3 analysis 2, AO4 evaluation 6. Level 3 (9–12): developed analysis in context plus a supported judgement that answers the question for this business (e.g. 'it depends on…' weighed, with a clear conclusion). Level 2 (5–8): developed analysis with some, limited or unsupported evaluation. Level 1 (1–4): knowledge and some application; little or no analysis.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define the term 'batch production'.
parts.answer: A method in which a group (batch) of identical products is made together, passing through each stage of production before the next batch, which may be different, is started.
parts.working: 1 mark: groups of identical items produced together; 1 mark: whole batch moves through each stage / machines reset between batches.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one advantage of flow production for a soft drinks manufacturer.
parts.answer: Bottles move continuously along an automated line, so very large volumes are produced at low unit cost (economies of scale); this lets the manufacturer sell at competitive prices in a mass market. Also accept: consistent quality, less labour needed.
parts.working: 1 mark for knowledge of the term/concept; up to 2 marks for explaining it in the context of the business (application).

stem: Tasty Foods is choosing a method for packing snacks. Labour-intensive method: fixed costs Rs 2,000,000 a month, variable cost Rs 180 per unit. Capital-intensive method: fixed costs Rs 6,000,000 a month, variable cost Rs 80 per unit.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the average cost per unit for each production method at an output of 50,000 units a month.
parts.answer: Labour-intensive: Rs 220; capital-intensive: Rs 200

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one reason why Tasty Foods might still choose the labour-intensive method.
parts.answer: If demand is uncertain and output might fall (e.g. to 30,000 units), the capital-intensive method's high fixed costs would make its unit cost higher; workers are also more flexible for producing different snack recipes in small batches. Also accept: capital cost/finance, local job reputation.
parts.working: 1 mark for knowledge of the term/concept; up to 2 marks for explaining it in the context of the business (application).

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Analyse one disadvantage of job production for a business that makes made-to-measure wedding dresses.
parts.answer: Each dress is unique and made by skilled tailors, so labour cost per dress is high and economies of scale are not possible; the business must charge high prices, which limits its market to higher-income customers, and output is limited by the number of skilled tailors, restricting growth. Also accept: long lead times.
parts.working: Chain: unique/skilled/slow → high unit cost, low output → high price/limited market/growth. Marks: knowledge 1, application 1, analysis 3. Level 2 (3–5): a developed chain of analysis (cause → effect → impact) applied to this business. Level 1 (1–2): knowledge with limited application; no developed analysis.

stem: Ravi Tea Packers is considering an automated packing line costing Rs 30 million. It would replace 8 packing workers, each costing Rs 900,000 a year. The machine would cost Rs 1,200,000 a year to maintain.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the annual net saving and the payback period of the automated packing line.
parts.answer: Annual net saving Rs 6,000,000; payback 5 years.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Evaluate whether Ravi Tea Packers should automate its packing line.
parts.answer: For: Rs 6 million net annual saving; faster, consistent filling weights and hygiene meet supermarket requirements; capacity rises for growth; less dependence on labour. Against: payback of 5 years is long — the machine may be outdated or breakdowns occur; Rs 30 million may need a loan at high interest; 8 redundancies damage morale and the firm's local reputation and may cost redundancy pay; loss of flexibility for small orders of different pack sizes; technical skills needed for maintenance. Judgement: automate if demand is stable or growing and finance is available at reasonable cost, with redeployment of staff to reduce resistance; otherwise delay or lease the equipment. Consider whether 5-year payback is acceptable given the machine's expected life (e.g. 10 years).
parts.working: Use calculation; financial and non-financial factors; finance; workforce; judgement. Mark scheme: AO1 knowledge 2, AO2 application 2, AO3 analysis 2, AO4 evaluation 6. Level 3 (9–12): developed analysis in context plus a supported judgement that answers the question for this business (e.g. 'it depends on…' weighed, with a clear conclusion). Level 2 (5–8): developed analysis with some, limited or unsupported evaluation. Level 1 (1–4): knowledge and some application; little or no analysis.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Mehr Plastics must choose a site for a new factory. Forecast annual output is 150,000 units, sold at Rs 400 each. Site X: annual fixed costs Rs 18 million; variable cost Rs 250 per unit. Site Y: annual fixed costs Rs 24 million; variable cost Rs 220 per unit.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the forecast annual profit at each site.
parts.answer: Site X: Rs 4,500,000; Site Y: Rs 3,000,000

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the annual output at which both sites would have the same total costs.
parts.answer: 200,000 units

author: HomiLabs

stem: Zenith Garments is choosing between two sites. Factors and weights: labour cost 0.3; transport links 0.25; access to markets 0.25; government incentives 0.2. Scores out of 10 — Faisalabad: 8, 6, 7, 5. Karachi: 6, 9, 8, 4.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the weighted score for each site and state which site should be chosen on this basis.
parts.answer: Faisalabad 6.65; Karachi 6.85: Karachi has the higher score.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one limitation of using weighted scoring to choose a location.
parts.answer: The weights and scores are subjective: if managers gave labour cost a weight of 0.4 instead of 0.3, Faisalabad might win; the decision can be biased by managers' opinions and the method ignores factors not included, such as security or quality of life for staff.
parts.working: 1 mark for knowledge of the term/concept; up to 2 marks for explaining it in the context of the business (application).

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: FastTrack Logistics has grown from 200 to 2,500 employees in four years and now operates in 30 cities. Analyse two diseconomies of scale it may experience.
parts.answer: 1. Communication problems: with more layers and depots across 30 cities, messages from head office take longer and get distorted, so decisions (e.g. rerouting deliveries during floods) are slow, increasing costs and late deliveries. 2. Coordination and control problems / low motivation: managers cannot monitor all depots, so procedures differ and errors increase; employees in a large firm may feel remote from management, lowering motivation and raising labour turnover and absenteeism, increasing average costs.
parts.working: Diseconomies: communication, coordination/control, motivation/alienation; each linked to rising unit costs in context. Mark scheme: AO1 knowledge 2, AO2 application 2, AO3 analysis 4. Level 2 (5–8): two developed chains of analysis, each clearly applied to this business. Level 1 (1–4): knowledge and/or application with undeveloped or generic analysis. Evaluation earns no extra marks.

stem: GlobalToys is a multinational toy maker with all its production in southern China. It sells mainly in the USA and Europe. Labour costs in Pakistan are about 40 % lower than at its Chinese plants, but labour productivity is about 30 % lower. The US recently raised tariffs on some goods made in China.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate whether GlobalToys should move part of its production from China to Pakistan.
parts.answer: For: labour costs about 40 % lower; reduces dependence on one country (supply-chain risk, tariffs on Chinese goods in the US market); Pakistan has preferential (GSP+) access to EU markets for many exports and a large young workforce; government incentives in special economic zones. Against: with productivity 30 % lower, labour cost per unit is only about 14 % lower (0.6 ÷ 0.7 ≈ 0.86), not 40 %, and fewer skilled toy-making suppliers may raise other costs; infrastructure (power outages, ports) and political/economic instability; exchange-rate risk; set-up and relocation costs and redundancy in China; quality control at a distance; reputation risks if working conditions are poor. Judgement: a partial move (a second plant for simple, labour-intensive products) reduces risk and may cut costs, but only if productivity, power supply and quality standards can be assured; a full move is too risky.
parts.working: Quantitative and qualitative location factors; offshoring risks; partial vs full move; judgement. Mark scheme: AO1 knowledge 2, AO2 application 2, AO3 analysis 2, AO4 evaluation 6. Level 3 (9–12): developed analysis in context plus a supported judgement that answers the question for this business (e.g. 'it depends on…' weighed, with a clear conclusion). Level 2 (5–8): developed analysis with some, limited or unsupported evaluation. Level 1 (1–4): knowledge and some application; little or no analysis.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define the term 'added value'.
parts.answer: The difference between the selling price of a product and the cost of the bought-in materials and components used to make it.
parts.working: 1 mark: selling price (or sales revenue); 1 mark: minus cost of bought-in materials/inputs.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one way a coffee shop could increase the value it adds.
parts.answer: Create a relaxing atmosphere with comfortable seating and free Wi-Fi, so customers are willing to pay a higher price for each coffee while the cost of the beans and milk is unchanged; the difference (added value) increases. Also accept: branding, premium ingredients, latte art, speed/convenience.
parts.working: 1 mark for knowledge of the term/concept; up to 2 marks for explaining it in the context of the business (application).

stem: Craftwood makes dining tables. Each table sells for Rs 45,000. The wood, glue and polish for each table cost Rs 18,000. Craftwood sells 120 tables a month.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the added value per table and the total added value per month.
parts.answer: Rs 27,000 per table; Rs 3,240,000 per month

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why added value is not the same as profit.
parts.answer: Added value only subtracts the cost of bought-in materials (wood, polish); the business must still pay wages, rent, electricity and other overheads from the added value, so profit is lower than added value.
parts.working: 1 mark: added value = price − bought-in materials; 1 mark: other costs (labour, overheads) still to be paid; 1 mark: application.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate whether improving efficiency is more important than improving effectiveness for a courier company.
parts.answer: Efficiency (using fewer resources per parcel — fuel, riders' time, route optimisation) lowers unit costs, essential in a price-competitive market with thin margins. Effectiveness (achieving objectives such as on-time, undamaged delivery and customer satisfaction) wins and keeps business customers such as online retailers. Conflict: maximising parcels per rider may increase late or damaged deliveries. Judgement: for a courier, effectiveness (reliability) is the basis of its reputation and contracts, so it is more important; efficiency improvements are valuable only if they do not reduce reliability. Depends on its competitive strategy (low-cost vs premium express) and customers' priorities.
parts.working: Definitions of efficiency, effectiveness (and productivity); trade-offs; context; judgement. Mark scheme: AO1 knowledge 2, AO2 application 2, AO3 analysis 2, AO4 evaluation 6. Level 3 (9–12): developed analysis in context plus a supported judgement that answers the question for this business (e.g. 'it depends on…' weighed, with a clear conclusion). Level 2 (5–8): developed analysis with some, limited or unsupported evaluation. Level 1 (1–4): knowledge and some application; little or no analysis.

stem: A shop refit consists of four activities. A: remove old fittings (3 days), starts at once. B: install new shelving (5 days), after A. C: rewire lighting (4 days), after A. D: paint and clean (2 days), after both B and C.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify the critical path and state the minimum time needed to complete the project.
parts.answer: A → B → D; 10 days.
parts.working: Paths: A–B–D = 3 + 5 + 2 = 10; A–C–D = 3 + 4 + 2 = 9 (M1). Critical path A–B–D, 10 days (A1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the total float for activity C.
parts.answer: 1 day
parts.working: C can start at day 3 and must finish by day 8 (latest start of D): float = 8 − 4 − 3 = 1 day (M1 A1).

author: HomiLabs

stem: A software company is installing a new ERP system. A: specify requirements (4 days), starts at once. B: order hardware (6 days), starts at once. C: configure software (3 days), after A. D: train staff (5 days), after A. E: install and test system (4 days), after B and C. F: go live and review (2 days), after D and E.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the earliest start time (EST) and latest finish time (LFT) of each activity.
parts.working: Forward pass: E starts after the later of B (6) and C (4+3 = 7) → 7; F after the later of D (9) and E (11) → 11; project ends day 13 (M1 A1). Backward pass from 13: LFT E = 11, D = 11, C = 7, B = 7, A = min(7 − 3, 11 − 5) = 4 (M1 A1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the critical path and the total float of activities B and D.
parts.answer: Critical path A–C–E–F (13 days). Float: B 1 day, D 2 days.
parts.working: Critical activities have zero float: A, C, E, F (B1). Float B = 7 − 6 − 0 = 1 (B1). Float D = 11 − 5 − 4 = 2 (B1).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Activity D is delayed by 3 days. State the effect on the project.
parts.answer: The project is delayed by 1 day (to 14 days).
parts.working: Delay 3 exceeds D's float of 2, so the project finishes 1 day late (B1).

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: MedSupply distributes medicines to 900 pharmacies. It plans to introduce an enterprise resource planning (ERP) system that links ordering, inventory, finance and delivery. Analyse two benefits of ERP for MedSupply.
parts.answer: 1. Better inventory control: real-time data on stock levels and expiry dates in every warehouse means medicines are reordered automatically when needed and older stock is sent first; fewer stock-outs at pharmacies and less waste of expired medicines, reducing costs. 2. Faster, more accurate order processing: an order from a pharmacy automatically updates inventory, invoices and delivery schedules, so errors fall and orders are delivered faster; customer satisfaction and cash flow (faster invoicing) improve. Costs of implementation and training should be noted but are not required.
parts.working: Benefits: integrated information, inventory control, efficiency, accuracy, customer service, better decision-making, cash flow. Mark scheme: AO1 knowledge 2, AO2 application 2, AO3 analysis 4. Level 2 (5–8): two developed chains of analysis, each clearly applied to this business. Level 1 (1–4): knowledge and/or application with undeveloped or generic analysis. Evaluation earns no extra marks.

stem: Prime Bags can make 12,000 bags a month and currently makes 9,000. It receives a new monthly order for 4,000 bags at Rs 560 each. The variable cost of making a bag itself is Rs 420; an outside supplier would make bags for Rs 510 each. Fixed costs will not change.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate Prime Bags' current capacity utilisation.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Prime Bags accepts the order, making 3,000 bags itself and outsourcing 1,000. Calculate the additional monthly profit from the order.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain one risk to Prime Bags of operating at 100 % capacity.
parts.answer: There is no spare time for machine maintenance, so breakdowns are more likely, and staff may be overworked, leading to mistakes and late deliveries to existing customers.
parts.working: 1 mark: risk identified; 1 mark: consequence.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Indus Crest Bank (an invented bank) employs 250 staff in its customer call centre in Lahore. A specialist overseas company has offered to run the call centre at 35 % lower cost. In a recent survey, only 58 % of the bank's customers were satisfied with telephone service.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate whether Indus Crest Bank should outsource its customer call centre to a specialist company in another country.
parts.answer: For: the specialist provider offers costs 35 % lower, 24-hour service and the ability to handle peaks; the bank can focus on its core banking activities and avoid investing in new call-centre technology. Against: loss of control over service quality — customer satisfaction is already a problem; language/accent and cultural differences may frustrate customers; data security and regulatory risks with customers' financial information sent abroad; negative publicity from 250 local job losses; dependence on one supplier and exchange-rate risk on contract costs. Judgement: outsourcing basic queries (balance checks, card blocking) may be sensible, but complex and high-value customer contact should stay in-house; the decision depends on the provider's security standards, contract terms (service-level agreements) and whether customer service is part of the bank's competitive advantage.
parts.working: Benefits and risks of outsourcing; quality, control, security, reputation, cost; judgement. Mark scheme: AO1 knowledge 2, AO2 application 2, AO3 analysis 2, AO4 evaluation 6. Level 3 (9–12): developed analysis in context plus a supported judgement that answers the question for this business (e.g. 'it depends on…' weighed, with a clear conclusion). Level 2 (5–8): developed analysis with some, limited or unsupported evaluation. Level 1 (1–4): knowledge and some application; little or no analysis.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Strategic implementation (culture, change, contingency, corporate plans)

parts.label: a
parts.text: BrightIdeas is an advertising agency in Karachi. Staff work in small project teams formed for each client campaign; team members are chosen for their expertise rather than seniority. Analyse two features of a task culture that are likely to benefit BrightIdeas.
parts.answer: 1. Focus on getting the job done through teams of experts: each campaign team brings together copywriters, designers and digital specialists, so creative problems are solved quickly and campaigns meet clients' briefs, helping BrightIdeas win repeat business. 2. Flexibility and power based on expertise rather than position: teams can be formed and disbanded as clients change, and junior staff with the best ideas are listened to; this encourages creativity and motivation, important in a competitive creative industry.
parts.working: Features of task culture (Handy): team-based, expertise-driven, flexible, results-focused; linked to an advertising agency. Mark scheme: AO1 knowledge 2, AO2 application 2, AO3 analysis 4. Level 2 (5–8): two developed chains of analysis, each clearly applied to this business. Level 1 (1–4): knowledge and/or application with undeveloped or generic analysis. Evaluation earns no extra marks.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Strategic implementation (culture, change, contingency, corporate plans)

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the term 'role culture', using Pak Postal Services (a large state-owned organisation) as an example.
parts.answer: A culture in which people work within clearly defined roles, rules and procedures in a hierarchical structure; power comes from a person's position. At Pak Postal Services, staff follow set procedures for handling mail and decisions pass up the hierarchy.
parts.working: 1 mark: clearly defined roles/rules/procedures; 1 mark: hierarchy/power from position (bureaucracy); 1 mark: application.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one problem of a role culture if Pak Postal Services wants to compete with private courier companies.
parts.answer: Role cultures are slow to change: new ideas such as same-day parcel delivery must pass through many levels and procedures, so private couriers launch new services first and win customers.
parts.working: 1 mark for knowledge of the term/concept; up to 2 marks for explaining it in the context of the business (application).

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Strategic implementation (culture, change, contingency, corporate plans)

parts.label: a
parts.text: CityHealth, a group of 6 private hospitals, is introducing a new electronic patient-records system. It has appointed a senior doctor as project champion. Analyse two benefits to CityHealth of appointing a project champion for this change.
parts.answer: 1. Overcoming resistance: a respected senior doctor can explain the benefits of electronic records to other doctors and nurses, who may trust a colleague more than IT managers; resistance falls and staff use the system properly, so the change succeeds faster. 2. Driving the project through obstacles: the champion has authority to secure resources (training time, IT support) and solve problems between departments, keeping the project on schedule and within budget, reducing disruption to patient care.
parts.working: Role of project champion: advocacy, overcoming resistance, securing resources, communication, maintaining momentum. Mark scheme: AO1 knowledge 2, AO2 application 2, AO3 analysis 4. Level 2 (5–8): two developed chains of analysis, each clearly applied to this business. Level 1 (1–4): knowledge and/or application with undeveloped or generic analysis. Evaluation earns no extra marks.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Strategic implementation (culture, change, contingency, corporate plans)

parts.label: a
parts.text: Analyse two reasons why QuickBite, an online food-delivery platform operating in 8 cities, needs a contingency plan.
parts.answer: 1. Dependence on technology: if the app or payment system crashes (e.g. cyber attack, server failure), no orders can be taken; a plan with backup servers and procedures restores service quickly, limiting lost revenue and protecting trust. 2. External disruption: floods, fuel shortages or riders' strikes could stop deliveries in a city; a plan for alternative riders, communication with customers and restaurants reduces disruption and reputational damage, and helps QuickBite recover faster than rivals.
parts.working: Reasons: unexpected events (IT failure, natural disaster, supplier failure, strikes), protect reputation, faster recovery, stakeholder confidence. Mark scheme: AO1 knowledge 2, AO2 application 2, AO3 analysis 4. Level 2 (5–8): two developed chains of analysis, each clearly applied to this business. Level 1 (1–4): knowledge and/or application with undeveloped or generic analysis. Evaluation earns no extra marks.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Strategic implementation (culture, change, contingency, corporate plans)

parts.label: a
parts.text: Analyse two benefits of a corporate plan for Shalimar Hospitality Group, which owns 9 hotels and plans to open 6 more by 2030.
parts.answer: 1. Clear direction and coordination: the corporate plan sets the group's mission, objectives (e.g. 6 new hotels, 70 % occupancy) and strategy, so each hotel and department (marketing, HR, finance) works towards the same targets and resources are allocated consistently. 2. Helps secure finance and monitor progress: banks and investors can see the planned growth and forecasts, making it easier to raise finance for new hotels; managers can compare actual results with the plan and take corrective action early.
parts.working: Benefits: direction, coordination, resource allocation, finance, control/review, motivation. Mark scheme: AO1 knowledge 2, AO2 application 2, AO3 analysis 4. Level 2 (5–8): two developed chains of analysis, each clearly applied to this business. Level 1 (1–4): knowledge and/or application with undeveloped or generic analysis. Evaluation earns no extra marks.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Strategic implementation (culture, change, contingency, corporate plans)
stem: AirPak (an invented state-owned airline) has made losses for ten years and is being sold to private investors. It employs 7,000 people, has a strong trade union and a bureaucratic culture. The new owners plan to cut costs and change working practices quickly.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate whether Kotter's 8-step model would help AirPak manage the change to private ownership successfully.
parts.answer: Helpful: steps such as creating urgency (heavy losses), forming a guiding coalition of managers and union leaders, communicating a clear vision (reliable, profitable airline), empowering staff and generating short-term wins (e.g. on-time performance improvements) would address resistance among 7,000 employees who fear job losses; anchoring change in culture tackles the long-standing bureaucratic culture. Limitations: the model is linear and time-consuming, while the new owners want quick cost cuts; it does not remove the real conflict over redundancies; success depends on leadership credibility and union cooperation; external factors (fuel prices, competition) may undermine short-term wins. Judgement: the model provides a useful framework, especially for communication and culture, but must be combined with negotiation over jobs and a realistic timetable.
parts.working: Kotter's steps applied; resistance; culture; limitations of the model; judgement. Mark scheme: AO1 knowledge 2, AO2 application 2, AO3 analysis 2, AO4 evaluation 6. Level 3 (9–12): developed analysis in context plus a supported judgement that answers the question for this business (e.g. 'it depends on…' weighed, with a clear conclusion). Level 2 (5–8): developed analysis with some, limited or unsupported evaluation. Level 1 (1–4): knowledge and some application; little or no analysis.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Strategic implementation (culture, change, contingency, corporate plans)
stem: Nexus Insurance (an invented company) employs 420 staff at its head office in Lahore. To reduce rent and be closer to regulators, it plans to move the head office to Islamabad in 12 months. A staff survey shows 60 % of employees do not want to move.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate the most effective way for Nexus Insurance to overcome employee resistance to moving its head office from Lahore to Islamabad.
parts.answer: Causes of resistance: fear of the unknown, family disruption, cost of moving, loss of social ties. Methods: (1) Communication and education — explain reasons (closer to regulators, lower rent) early; (2) Participation — involve staff in planning the move; (3) Support — relocation allowances, help with housing and schools; (4) Negotiation — extra pay or options to transfer/redundancy packages; (5) Coercion — imposing the move, quick but damages morale and leads to loss of skilled staff. Judgement: a combination of early communication, participation and financial support is most effective, because the main resistance comes from personal costs to families; negotiation is needed for key staff; coercion should be avoided as Nexus relies on experienced underwriters who could join rivals.
parts.working: Causes of resistance; methods (e.g. Kotter & Schlesinger); suitability in context; judgement. Mark scheme: AO1 knowledge 2, AO2 application 2, AO3 analysis 2, AO4 evaluation 6. Level 3 (9–12): developed analysis in context plus a supported judgement that answers the question for this business (e.g. 'it depends on…' weighed, with a clear conclusion). Level 2 (5–8): developed analysis with some, limited or unsupported evaluation. Level 1 (1–4): knowledge and some application; little or no analysis.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Strategic implementation (culture, change, contingency, corporate plans)
stem: NorthTrails is a tour operator with 12 employees that runs trekking and sightseeing tours in Gilgit-Baltistan. Last year a landslide closed the main road for 9 days during peak season.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate whether contingency planning is worth the cost for NorthTrails, a small tour operator.
parts.answer: Worth it: tours in mountainous areas face landslides, road closures, extreme weather and security alerts; a plan (alternative routes, emergency contacts, insurance, refund policies, communication templates) protects customers' safety and the firm's reputation; it reduces losses and recovery time; may be required by insurers or international partners. Costs/limits: time and money for a small business; cannot predict every crisis; plans must be updated and staff trained; low-probability events may not justify heavy spending. Judgement: given the high risks and the importance of safety and reputation for a tour operator, a simple, low-cost plan focused on the most likely and most damaging events is worth it; extensive planning for unlikely events is not.
parts.working: Benefits/costs of contingency planning; risk assessment (likelihood × impact); context; judgement. Mark scheme: AO1 knowledge 2, AO2 application 2, AO3 analysis 2, AO4 evaluation 6. Level 3 (9–12): developed analysis in context plus a supported judgement that answers the question for this business (e.g. 'it depends on…' weighed, with a clear conclusion). Level 2 (5–8): developed analysis with some, limited or unsupported evaluation. Level 1 (1–4): knowledge and some application; little or no analysis.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Strategic implementation (culture, change, contingency, corporate plans)
stem: United Prime Bank (an invented bank), a large, traditional bank with a hierarchical structure, has taken over Orbit Bank, a small digital bank whose young staff work in flexible teams. The aim is to grow digital banking and cut costs by 15 %.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate whether changing corporate culture is essential to the success of the merger between United Prime Bank and Orbit Bank.
parts.answer: Essential: the banks have very different cultures (United Prime: hierarchical, risk-averse, role culture; Orbit: young, digital, task culture); without a shared culture, staff may clash, decision-making slows, key digital staff may leave, and the expected cost savings and digital growth may not be achieved — many mergers fail because of culture clashes. Not alone essential: success also depends on integrating IT systems, retaining customers, the price paid, economic conditions and regulation; a single culture may not be needed — the digital unit could keep its own culture as a separate division. Judgement: some cultural integration (shared values, customer focus) is essential, but forcing one culture on all staff could destroy Orbit's strengths; management should create a common core while allowing sub-cultures.
parts.working: Culture types (Handy), culture clash in mergers, other success factors; judgement. Mark scheme: AO1 knowledge 2, AO2 application 2, AO3 analysis 2, AO4 evaluation 6. subtopic: Strategic implementation (culture, change, contingency, corporate plans)
stem: LearnHub is an EdTech company in Lahore offering online tutoring for school students. Its users grew from 50,000 to 200,000 in two years. It plans to enter Bangladesh and the Gulf and must raise more finance from investors.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate the importance of a corporate plan to the future success of LearnHub.
parts.answer: Important: LearnHub is growing fast (users ×4 in two years) and entering new countries; a corporate plan sets clear objectives, allocates limited funds between product development, marketing and expansion, coordinates departments and reassures investors who are asked for more finance. Limitations: EdTech markets change rapidly (AI tutoring, regulation), so a rigid plan may become outdated; success depends more on product quality, user growth and the founders' agility; planning takes time. Judgement: a flexible corporate plan with regular review (and contingency plans) is important, particularly for raising finance and managing growth, but it must be adapted as the market changes; it is necessary but not sufficient.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Strategic implementation (culture, change, contingency, corporate plans)
stem:
ValueMart (an invented supermarket chain) has 40 stores in Pakistan. Timeline:
2021: Sales fall 8 % as online grocers grow. CEO announces closure of 6 stores and an online service, without consulting staff. Two-week strike in 10 stores.
2022: Appoints a project champion; online pilot in Karachi succeeds (2,000 orders a day).
2023: Online service launched in all cities within 3 months. App crashes repeatedly; complaints triple; operating profit falls 20 %.
2024: Staff retraining programme for 1,500 employees; new app version.
2025: Online sales 18 % of revenue; total revenue up 9 % on 2021; store-manager labour turnover 25 % (12 % in 2021).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate the effectiveness of ValueMart's management of change between 2021 and 2025.
parts.answer: Effective aspects: a clear reason for change (online competition, falling sales); a project champion and pilot in 2022 created a short-term win; online sales grew to 18 % of revenue by 2025; staff retraining helped. Ineffective aspects: the 2021 announcement without consultation caused a two-week strike in 10 stores; the rollout in 2023 was rushed — the app crashed and customer complaints rose; labour turnover among store managers rose to 25 %, losing experience; profit fell in 2023. Judgement: change was eventually achieved (online channel built, revenue recovering), but poorly managed in the early stages — lack of communication and participation (Kotter steps 1–4 missed) raised costs and delayed benefits; overall partially effective. External factors (e.g. inflation, the growth of online rivals) may also have affected results.
parts.working: Use timeline data; apply change-management concepts (Kotter, resistance, project champions); weigh evidence; judgement on effectiveness. Levels: Level 4 (16–20): accurate knowledge, strong use of the case data, three or four developed chains of analysis and a well-supported judgement/recommendation throughout, specific to this business and its situation. Level 3 (11–15): developed analysis in context with some supported evaluation. Level 2 (6–10): some analysis, mostly descriptive use of the case; evaluation weak or unsupported. Level 1 (1–5): knowledge with little application.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Strategic implementation (culture, change, contingency, corporate plans)
stem: ConnectNet (an invented mobile network) has 30 million subscribers. Appendix 1: in May 2025 a cyber attack shut down its network for 3 days; it had no tested contingency plan. Appendix 2: it took 20 hours to issue a public statement; social media complaints reached 400,000. Appendix 3: the regulator fined it Rs 1.2 billion; 4 % of subscribers moved to rivals within 3 months. Appendix 4: a full backup data centre would cost Rs 3 billion; annual profit is Rs 9 billion.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Advise ConnectNet on how it should improve its contingency planning and crisis management over the next two years.
parts.answer: Analysis of the 2025 crisis: no tested plan; 3-day outage; slow, unclear communication; regulator fine and 4 % of customers lost. Options: (1) IT resilience — backup data centres, cyber-security investment, regular penetration testing (high cost Rs 3 billion but reduces probability and impact); (2) Crisis management team and communication plan — pre-prepared messages, a spokesperson, compensation policy; (3) Scenario planning and regular simulations; (4) Insurance against cyber risk. Recommendation: prioritise risk assessment (likelihood × impact) and a tested crisis communication plan immediately (low cost, high impact on reputation), followed by phased investment in IT resilience; justify with appendix data on customer losses, fines and costs; consider finance, the competitive market (customers can switch easily) and the need for board-level responsibility.
parts.working: Use appendices; distinguish contingency planning and crisis management; prioritised, justified recommendation. Levels: Level 4 (16–20): accurate knowledge, strong use of the case data, three or four developed chains of analysis and a well-supported judgement/recommendation throughout, specific to this business and its situation. Level 1 (1–5): knowledge with little application.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Strategic implementation (culture, change, contingency, corporate plans)
stem:
Rehbar Group (an invented conglomerate) owns a textile division. Timeline:
2020: Founder makes all major decisions personally; division enters home textiles quickly; revenue Rs 8 billion.
2021–22: Two senior managers leave, saying ideas are ignored. European buyers ask for sustainable fabrics; the division does not respond. Revenue falls to Rs 6.9 billion.
2023: New CEO creates cross-functional product teams and delegates decisions to them. Absenteeism rises among long-serving staff.
2024–25: Product development time falls from 9 months to 5 months. Export orders up 30 %. The rupee falls 18 % against the euro. Revenue Rs 9.6 billion in 2025.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate the impact of corporate culture on the performance of Rehbar Group's textile division between 2020 and 2025.
parts.answer: Evidence: the power culture under the founder (2020–22) allowed fast decisions and a successful entry into home textiles, but discouraged ideas from managers — two senior managers left and the division missed the shift to sustainable fabrics demanded by buyers. After 2023 the new CEO introduced a more task-based culture (cross-functional teams, delegated authority): product development time fell from 9 to 5 months, export orders rose 30 %. However, older staff resisted, absenteeism rose in 2023, and some performance gains came from the weaker rupee (making exports cheaper). Judgement: culture had a major impact — the power culture contributed to stagnation and the move to a task culture helped recovery — but external factors (exchange rate, buyer demand) also explain performance, so culture was important but not the only factor.
parts.working: Culture types (power, role, task, person), change of culture, evidence from timeline, other factors; judgement. Levels: Level 4 (16–20): accurate knowledge, strong use of the case data, three or four developed chains of analysis and a well-supported judgement/recommendation throughout, specific to this business and its situation. Level 1 (1–5): knowledge with little application.

subtopic: Strategic implementation (culture, change, contingency, corporate plans)
stem: Sweet Treats Ltd (an invented company) is a family-owned maker of traditional sweets (mithai) in Lahore. Appendix 1: the board has decided to enter the UK market. Appendix 2: all decisions are made by the two founding brothers; staff are rarely consulted. Appendix 3: UK distributors say products must meet strict food-labelling and hygiene standards; two distributors of South Asian foods are interested. Appendix 4: budget for UK entry Rs 150 million; £1 = Rs 360 and the rate has changed by up to 12 % in a year.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Advise the owners of Sweet Treats Ltd on how to implement their strategy of entering the UK market successfully.
parts.answer: Key implementation issues: (1) Corporate plan — clear objectives (sales of £2 million in 3 years), budget and milestones; (2) Culture — the family-run power culture may slow decisions; delegating authority to a UK manager and building a team culture would help; (3) Project champion/team — appoint a senior manager to lead entry, liaise with UK distributors and food-safety regulators; (4) Change management — staff in Pakistan need training in export quality standards (UK food labelling, hygiene); communicate the reasons for change to reduce resistance; (5) Contingency planning — currency risk, failure to meet standards, supply disruption. Recommendation: appoint a project champion and a small cross-functional export team, start with a pilot through ethnic grocery chains in cities with a large South Asian population before mainstream supermarkets, with a contingency plan for exchange-rate and shipping risks; justify with appendices (finance limits, family control, survey of UK distributors).
parts.working: Implementation tools: business/corporate plans, culture, project champions, change management, contingency planning; recommendation tied to case data. Levels: Level 4 (16–20): accurate knowledge, strong use of the case data, three or four developed chains of analysis and a well-supported judgement/recommendation throughout, specific to this business and its situation. author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Strategic implementation (culture, change, contingency, corporate plans)
stem: Al-Fajr University (an invented private university). Corporate plan 2020–2025 objectives: (1) 12,000 students by 2025 (8,000 in 2020); (2) open a medical college by 2023; (3) double research income; (4) raise graduate employment to 75 %. Results 2025: 10,800 students; medical college opened 2023; research income up 20 %; graduate employment 74 % (62 % in 2020). The plan was not revised during the period, although the economy slowed in 2023 and two online universities entered the market. Academic staff turnover was 18 % a year.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate the effectiveness of the corporate plan of Al-Fajr University between 2020 and 2025.
parts.answer: Objectives and outcomes: student numbers target 12,000 by 2025 — achieved 10,800 (90 %); new medical college opened on time (2023) — success; research income target missed; graduate employment improved from 62 % to 74 %. Strengths: the plan gave clear direction for major projects (the medical college opened on time) and coordinated faculties. Weaknesses: the plan was never revised when two online universities entered the market and the economy slowed in 2023, which probably explains the shortfall in students; academic staff turnover of 18 % a year suggests low commitment and makes research targets harder to reach. Judgement: moderately effective — it delivered major projects and graduate outcomes, but rigidity and lack of review/contingency reduced its effectiveness; a plan needs regular review and staff involvement. Use criteria: achievement of objectives, flexibility, stakeholder involvement.
parts.working: Assess against plan objectives using data; corporate plan benefits and limitations; external changes; judgement. Levels: Level 4 (16–20): accurate knowledge, strong use of the case data, three or four developed chains of analysis and a well-supported judgement/recommendation throughout, specific to this business and its situation. author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Strategic choice (Ansoff, decision trees, force field)
stem: Zaiqa Foods is choosing between two options. Launch a new frozen-meal range: cost Rs 5 million; probability 0.6 of high demand (return Rs 14 million) and 0.4 of low demand (return Rs 4 million). Upgrade its existing range: cost Rs 2 million; probability 0.7 of success (return Rs 6 million) and 0.3 of failure (return Rs 3 million).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the expected net value of each option and state which option Zaiqa Foods should choose on financial grounds.
parts.answer: New product: Rs 5.0 million; upgrade: Rs 3.1 million — choose the new product.
parts.working: New product: 0.6 × 14 + 0.4 × 4 = 10.0; − 5 = Rs 5.0m (M1 A1). Upgrade: 0.7 × 6 + 0.3 × 3 = 5.1; − 2 = Rs 3.1m (M1). Choose the new product (A1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one limitation of using a decision tree for this decision.
parts.answer: The probabilities and payoffs are estimates (e.g. the 0.6 chance of high demand); if they are wrong, the 'best' option may change. The method also ignores qualitative factors such as brand image.
parts.working: 1 mark: limitation; 1 mark: explained.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Strategic choice (Ansoff, decision trees, force field)
stem: Metro Cabs is considering replacing its petrol taxis with electric vehicles. Its managers scored the forces (1 = weak, 5 = strong). Driving forces: lower running costs 4; government subsidy 3; customer demand for greener transport 5. Restraining forces: high purchase cost 3; lack of charging points 4; drivers' resistance 2; uncertain battery life 2.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the total score for the driving forces and for the restraining forces.
parts.answer: Driving forces 12; restraining forces 11.
parts.working: Driving: 4 + 3 + 5 = 12 (B1). Restraining: 3 + 4 + 2 + 2 = 11 (B1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain whether the force field analysis suggests that Metro Cabs should introduce electric vehicles.
parts.answer: Driving forces (12) slightly exceed restraining forces (11), so the analysis suggests going ahead; but the margin is small and the scores are subjective, so Metro Cabs should try to reduce the main restraining force — lack of charging points (score 4) — e.g. by installing chargers at depots, before proceeding.
parts.working: 1 mark: driving > restraining → proceed; 1 mark: small margin/subjective; 1 mark: action to strengthen drivers or weaken restraints.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Strategic choice (Ansoff, decision trees, force field)

parts.label: a
parts.text: Using Ansoff's matrix, analyse two risks for Lahore Cement Company of diversifying into a chain of furniture stores.
parts.answer: 1. Lack of market and product knowledge: diversification means a new product in a new market; the company's skills are in heavy manufacturing and selling to builders, not retailing furniture to households, so poor decisions on design, location and pricing could lead to losses. 2. Diverting resources and finance: the investment needed for stores and inventory could weaken the core cement business (e.g. less money for new kilns), and if the furniture chain fails, the company's overall profit and share price could fall. Ansoff identifies diversification as the highest-risk strategy.
parts.working: Risks: unfamiliar product and market, no synergy, finance/opportunity cost, management overstretch, brand. Mark scheme: AO1 knowledge 2, AO2 application 2, AO3 analysis 4. Level 2 (5–8): two developed chains of analysis, each clearly applied to this business. Level 1 (1–4): knowledge and/or application with undeveloped or generic analysis. Evaluation earns no extra marks.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Strategic choice (Ansoff, decision trees, force field)
stem: Bookworm, a bookshop chain, is choosing between opening a new branch in Islamabad (cost Rs 20 million) and launching an online platform (cost Rs 8 million). Forecast returns (Rs million) and probabilities — Branch: high demand 50 (0.3); medium 28 (0.5); low 10 (0.2). Online platform: high 24 (0.4); medium 15 (0.4); low 5 (0.2).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the expected net value of each option.
parts.answer: Branch: Rs 11.0 million; online platform: Rs 8.6 million.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one reason why Bookworm might choose the online platform despite the result.
parts.answer: The online platform has a much lower cost (Rs 8m vs Rs 20m) and lower risk — in the worst case it loses Rs 3m rather than Rs 10m — which matters if Bookworm's finance is limited.
parts.working: 1 mark: risk/finance argument; 1 mark: supported with figures.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Strategic choice (Ansoff, decision trees, force field)
stem: Skyline Developers owns a plot of land in Islamabad. Option 1: sell the land now for a certain Rs 110 million. Option 2: build apartments at a cost of Rs 300 million; the probability of strong demand is 0.65 (total sales Rs 520 million) and of weak demand 0.35 (total sales Rs 260 million).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the expected net value of building the apartments.
parts.answer: Rs 129 million (compared with Rs 110 million for selling the land).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Evaluate whether Skyline Developers should use the decision tree result to decide to build the apartments.
parts.answer: For: building gives a higher expected value (Rs 129m vs a certain Rs 110m); decision trees make the options, risks and probabilities explicit and comparable. Against: the advantage is small (Rs 19m) compared with the risk — if demand is weak the project loses Rs 40m (260 − 300), whereas selling is certain; the probabilities (0.65) are estimates based on a housing market affected by interest rates; costs may overrun; expected value is an average that would only occur over many decisions, not a one-off project; qualitative factors such as the firm's cash position, reputation, staff and risk attitude of owners are ignored. Judgement: the decision tree is useful but should not decide alone; given the small difference and the downside risk, Skyline should build only if it can afford a loss and has confidence in the demand forecast (e.g. pre-sales of apartments).
parts.working: Use the calculation; limitations of decision trees (estimates, averages, ignores qualitative factors, risk attitude); judgement. Mark scheme: AO1 knowledge 2, AO2 application 2, AO3 analysis 2, AO4 evaluation 6. Level 3 (9–12): developed analysis in context plus a supported judgement that answers the question for this business (e.g. 'it depends on…' weighed, with a clear conclusion). Level 2 (5–8): developed analysis with some, limited or unsupported evaluation. Level 1 (1–4): knowledge and some application; little or no analysis.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Strategic choice (Ansoff, decision trees, force field)
stem: NectarJuice sells fruit juices in Pakistan and has 12 % of the market. It is choosing between selling its existing juices in the Gulf (market development) and launching energy drinks in Pakistan (product development).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate whether Ansoff's matrix would help NectarJuice choose between market development and product development.
parts.answer: Helpful: the matrix clarifies options and their relative risk — market development (selling existing juices in the Gulf) uses existing products and production know-how but requires knowledge of a new market; product development (new energy drinks at home) uses existing customer knowledge and distribution but needs R&D and faces strong competitors. It encourages structured thinking about risk. Limitations: it does not provide data on market size, costs or likely returns; it simplifies — both options may involve elements of 'newness'; it ignores the firm's resources and competitors' actions; risk depends on how new the market/product really is (the Gulf has a large Pakistani diaspora, reducing risk). Judgement: the matrix is a useful starting tool, but NectarJuice must combine it with market research, financial analysis (e.g. investment appraisal, decision trees) and SWOT before choosing.
parts.working: Ansoff concepts and risk; limitations; other tools needed; judgement. Mark scheme: AO1 knowledge 2, AO2 application 2, AO3 analysis 2, AO4 evaluation 6. Level 3 (9–12): developed analysis in context plus a supported judgement that answers the question for this business (e.g. 'it depends on…' weighed, with a clear conclusion). author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Strategic choice (Ansoff, decision trees, force field)
stem: Margalla Cement (an invented company). Appendix 1: domestic demand flat; capacity utilisation 68 %; gearing 52 %. Appendix 2: Option 1 — export cement to Central Asia: cost Rs 2.0 billion; probability of success 0.55 (return Rs 5.0 billion), failure 0.45 (return Rs 1.2 billion). Option 2 — set up a ready-mix concrete and construction services business in Pakistan: cost Rs 1.5 billion; probability of success 0.7 (return Rs 3.2 billion), failure 0.3 (return Rs 1.0 billion). Appendix 3: government plans large infrastructure spending over five years. Appendix 4: cement is heavy; road transport to Central Asia adds about 25 % to delivered cost; border closures occurred twice in the last three years.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Advise the board of Margalla Cement on which strategic option it should choose.
parts.answer: Decision tree: Option 1 (export to Central Asia — market development): 0.55 × 5.0 + 0.45 × 1.2 − 2.0 = Rs 1.29 billion. Option 2 (ready-mix concrete and construction services — related diversification/forward integration): 0.7 × 3.2 + 0.3 × 1.0 − 1.5 = Rs 1.04 billion. Option 1 has the higher expected value but more risk (worst case −0.8bn vs −0.5bn). Ansoff: market development uses existing products but new, politically and logistically risky markets; exchange-rate and transport costs (cement is heavy, Appendix 4). Option 2 uses existing customers and synergies (own cement), steadier demand from government infrastructure projects, lower investment. Force field / SWOT: strong domestic brand, overcapacity at home (capacity utilisation 68 %) — exports would use capacity directly. Recommendation: justified choice, e.g. Option 2 because of lower risk, synergy and current high gearing, possibly piloting exports on a small scale; or Option 1 if the board accepts risk to use capacity. Conditions and reliability of probabilities discussed.
parts.working: Use decision tree calculation, Ansoff, appendices (capacity, gearing, transport costs, political risk). Clear recommendation with conditions. Levels: Level 4 (16–20): accurate knowledge, strong use of the case data, three or four developed chains of analysis and a well-supported judgement/recommendation throughout, specific to this business and its situation. Level 1 (1–5): knowledge with little application.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Strategic choice (Ansoff, decision trees, force field)
stem: Atlas Pumps makes water pumps. Option A: expand its factory at a cost of Rs 40 million. If domestic demand grows (probability 0.6) the return is Rs 90 million. If it does not grow (0.4), Atlas will try to export the extra output: export success (0.5) returns Rs 60 million; export failure (0.5) returns Rs 20 million. Option B: subcontract extra production at a set-up cost of Rs 5 million; returns are Rs 45 million if demand grows (0.6) and Rs 15 million if it does not (0.4).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the expected net value of each option.
parts.answer: Expand: Rs 30 million; subcontract: Rs 28 million.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Evaluate whether Atlas Pumps should expand its factory.
parts.answer: Financial: expanding gives a slightly higher expected value (Rs 30m vs Rs 28m), but the difference is only Rs 2m and depends on several estimated probabilities, including the uncertain export-market outcome; the worst case for expansion is −Rs 20m (20 − 40) compared with +Rs 10m for subcontracting. Expansion requires Rs 40m investment, raising gearing or using scarce cash. Non-financial: expansion gives control over quality and capacity for long-term growth; subcontracting is flexible and low-risk but quality and delivery depend on another firm, and profit margins are lower. Judgement: because the expected values are nearly equal and expansion is far riskier, subcontracting is the better choice unless Atlas is confident about demand growth (e.g. firm orders) and can finance expansion easily; it could subcontract now and expand later when demand is proven.
parts.working: Use the two-stage decision tree; risk (worst outcomes), reliability of probabilities, finance, quality/control, flexibility; judgement. Mark scheme: AO1 knowledge 2, AO2 application 2, AO3 analysis 2, AO4 evaluation 6. Level 3 (9–12): developed analysis in context plus a supported judgement that answers the question for this business (e.g. 'it depends on…' weighed, with a clear conclusion). Level 2 (5–8): developed analysis with some, limited or unsupported evaluation. Level 1 (1–4): knowledge and some application; little or no analysis.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: FlyThrift is a new budget airline in Pakistan. Analyse two ways it could achieve a competitive advantage through cost leadership.
parts.answer: 1. Standardised fleet and high aircraft utilisation: using one aircraft type reduces training, spare-parts and maintenance costs; quick turnarounds mean each aircraft flies more hours a day, spreading fixed costs over more passengers, so FlyThrift can offer the lowest fares and still make a profit. 2. No-frills service and direct online sales: charging for bags and meals, and selling tickets only through its app, cuts costs and commission paid to travel agents; lower costs per seat allow lower fares than full-service airlines, attracting price-sensitive travellers and students.
parts.working: Porter's cost leadership: economies of scale, efficiency, standardisation, low overheads, online distribution; linked to fares and market share. Mark scheme: AO1 knowledge 2, AO2 application 2, AO3 analysis 4. Level 2 (5–8): two developed chains of analysis, each clearly applied to this business. Level 1 (1–4): knowledge and/or application with undeveloped or generic analysis. Evaluation earns no extra marks.

stem: DevSphere is a software house in Islamabad with 600 engineers. For 15 years it has specialised in secure software for banks; 70 % of its revenue comes from banks in the Middle East and Africa. Its prices are higher than many rivals', but it has never lost a major client.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate whether core competencies are the main source of competitive advantage for DevSphere.
parts.answer: Core competencies (Prahalad and Hamel): DevSphere's expertise in secure banking software, built over 15 years, is hard to copy, provides access to several markets (banks, insurance, fintech) and contributes significantly to customer benefits — meeting all three tests; this explains why it wins contracts against cheaper rivals. Other sources: long-term client relationships and switching costs, reputation, skilled staff (who could leave), lower costs from Pakistan-based development, government contracts. Risks: competencies can become 'core rigidities' if technology shifts (e.g. AI-based platforms); depends on retaining key engineers. Judgement: core competencies are the main source, but they rest on people and must be continually developed; relationships and cost advantages support them.
parts.working: Core competence theory and tests; other sources of advantage; sustainability; judgement. Mark scheme: AO1 knowledge 2, AO2 application 2, AO3 analysis 2, AO4 evaluation 6. author: HomiLabs

stem: CineStar operates 10 multiplex cinemas in large cities in Pakistan. Attendance has fallen 25 % in five years as streaming services have grown. Many smaller cities have no cinema at all.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate whether a blue ocean strategy would be successful for CineStar.
parts.answer: Blue ocean idea: create uncontested market space by offering a new combination of value (e.g. small 'family entertainment hubs' in smaller cities combining cinema, gaming and dining, at low prices with fewer, lower-cost screens) rather than competing head-to-head with streaming and large multiplexes (red ocean). Could succeed: smaller cities lack cinemas; families want affordable outings; reduce costs (fewer screens, no premium seating) and create new value (events, live sports screenings). Risks: easy to copy if successful; demand uncertain; requires investment and new skills; streaming remains strong; local power cuts and security. Judgement: a blue ocean approach could succeed if CineStar offers a genuinely new value combination in under-served towns and moves quickly; but it is risky and must be tested with pilots and market research.
parts.working: Blue ocean concepts (eliminate-reduce-raise-create, value innovation); context; risks; judgement. Mark scheme: AO1 knowledge 2, AO2 application 2, AO3 analysis 2, AO4 evaluation 6. Level 3 (9–12): developed analysis in context plus a supported judgement that answers the question for this business (e.g. 'it depends on…' weighed, with a clear conclusion). Level 2 (5–8): developed analysis with some, limited or unsupported evaluation. Level 1 (1–4): knowledge and some application; little or no analysis.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Unity Crest Bank (an invented mid-sized bank) has 180 branches. Appendix 1: its market share is 4 %; the three largest banks have 45 % together. Appendix 2: cost-to-income ratio 68 % (industry average 55 %). Appendix 3: a survey shows 58 % of small business owners are dissatisfied with their bank's service. Appendix 4: Islamic banking assets in Pakistan are growing about 20 % a year. Appendix 5: two digital-only banks now offer free accounts.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Advise the board of Unity Crest Bank whether to follow a strategy of differentiation or cost leadership over the next five years.
parts.answer: Cost leadership: digital banking, branch closures, automation could cut costs (cost-to-income ratio 68 % vs industry 55 %, Appendix 2); necessary to compete with digital banks offering low fees; but large banks have scale advantages and Unity Crest is mid-sized — it may not achieve the lowest costs. Differentiation: specialise in SME and agricultural lending with personal relationship managers, Islamic banking products, excellent service (Appendix 3: SMEs dissatisfied with current banks; Appendix 4: Islamic banking growing 20 % a year); allows higher margins and loyalty; but requires investment in skills and products and may be copied. Porter warns of being 'stuck in the middle'. Recommendation: focused differentiation on SMEs and Islamic banking, while cutting costs where it does not harm the differentiating features (digital processes for routine transactions); justify with appendix data; conditions (finance, staff skills, regulation).
parts.working: Porter's generic strategies (incl. focus), stuck in the middle; use appendices; justified recommendation. Levels: Level 4 (16–20): accurate knowledge, strong use of the case data, three or four developed chains of analysis and a well-supported judgement/recommendation throughout, specific to this business and its situation. Level 3 (11–15): developed analysis in context with some supported evaluation. Level 2 (6–10): some analysis, mostly descriptive use of the case; evaluation weak or unsupported. Level 1 (1–5): knowledge with little application.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Analyse how a PEST analysis could help Summit Tours plan its expansion into hotels in northern Pakistan.
parts.answer: Political/legal: identifying security conditions, government tourism policy and incentives (or planning restrictions in protected areas) helps Summit decide where and when to build and avoid costly delays. Economic: examining interest rates (cost of borrowing for construction), exchange rates (foreign tourists find Pakistan cheaper when the rupee falls) and domestic incomes helps forecast demand and finance costs. Social/Technological: rising domestic tourism among young urban families and online booking platforms shape the type of hotel and marketing. Any two developed factors showing how the analysis reduces risk and informs the decision earn full marks.
parts.working: Two PEST factors developed into consequences for the expansion decision (risk, demand, cost, timing). Mark scheme: AO1 knowledge 2, AO2 application 2, AO3 analysis 4. Level 2 (5–8): two developed chains of analysis, each clearly applied to this business. Level 1 (1–4): knowledge and/or application with undeveloped or generic analysis. Evaluation earns no extra marks.

stem: Daily Awaz Media Group (an invented company) publishes an Urdu newspaper and runs a news website. Print circulation has fallen 40 % in five years, while website visits have doubled. Online advertising revenue does not yet cover the fall in print revenue.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate the usefulness of a SWOT analysis to Daily Awaz Media Group in planning its future strategy.
parts.answer: Useful: brings together internal strengths (trusted Urdu brand, large journalist network) and weaknesses (declining print revenue, outdated IT), and external opportunities (growth in online video and mobile news) and threats (social media, falling print advertising); helps managers match strengths to opportunities (e.g. a paid digital news app) and identify urgent weaknesses. Limitations: it is a snapshot that can quickly become outdated in fast-changing media; it lists factors but does not rank or quantify them; subjective and possibly biased by managers' views; it does not itself produce a strategy — tools such as Ansoff, PEST, Porter's five forces and financial analysis are needed. Judgement: SWOT is a useful starting point for a business facing major change, but only if it is evidence-based, regularly updated and followed by detailed analysis of options.
parts.working: SWOT purpose and limitations; context of a declining print business; other tools; judgement. Mark scheme: AO1 knowledge 2, AO2 application 2, AO3 analysis 2, AO4 evaluation 6. Level 3 (9–12): developed analysis in context plus a supported judgement that answers the question for this business (e.g. 'it depends on…' weighed, with a clear conclusion). Level 2 (5–8): developed analysis with some, limited or unsupported evaluation. Level 1 (1–4): knowledge and some application; little or no analysis.

author: HomiLabs

stem: RideNow (an invented company) is a ride-hailing app in Pakistan with 20 % market share. Appendix 1: three rivals; fares fell 10 % last year in a price war. Appendix 2: 35 % of drivers stopped using RideNow last year; many drivers use two or three apps. Appendix 3: a large foreign ride-hailing company is planning to enter in 2027. Appendix 4: survey — 52 % of women passengers say safety is their main concern when choosing an app. Appendix 5: a new metro bus line has opened in two cities.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Using Porter's five forces and other strategic analysis, advise RideNow on its strategy for the next three years.
parts.answer: Five forces: rivalry is intense (three rivals, price wars — Appendix 1); buyer power is high (passengers switch apps easily, low switching costs); supplier power (drivers) is growing — drivers work for several apps and demand higher shares, and fuel costs rise; threat of substitutes (buses, metro, motorcycles, car-pooling) is moderate to high; threat of entry is moderate (capital needed for marketing, but technology is easy to copy; a foreign app is planning entry). The industry is structurally unattractive for pure price competition. Options: (1) differentiation — safety features for women passengers, reliable service, loyalty schemes, reducing buyer power; (2) driver loyalty programme (fuel cards, insurance) to reduce supplier power; (3) diversify into deliveries/payments to use its network (related diversification); (4) cost leadership — difficult against larger rivals. Recommendation: focus on differentiation and driver retention, expand into food/parcel deliveries in existing cities; justify using appendices (survey: safety concerns 52 %, driver churn 35 %), with limitations of five-forces analysis (static, industry-level).
parts.working: Apply all five forces with evidence; link to strategic options; justified recommendation; awareness of limitations. Levels: Level 4 (16–20): accurate knowledge, strong use of the case data, three or four developed chains of analysis and a well-supported judgement/recommendation throughout, specific to this business and its situation. Level 3 (11–15): developed analysis in context with some supported evaluation. Level 2 (6–10): some analysis, mostly descriptive use of the case; evaluation weak or unsupported. Level 1 (1–5): knowledge with little application.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define the term 'democratic leadership'.
parts.answer: A leadership style in which the leader involves employees in decision-making, discussing options and taking their views into account, although the leader may still make the final decision.
parts.working: 1 mark: leader involves/consults subordinates in decisions; 1 mark: two-way communication / staff views influence the final decision.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one difference between a leader and a manager, using the head teacher of a primary school in Abbottabad as an example.
