parts.answer: A manager plans, organises and controls resources to meet set targets (e.g. timetables, budgets, staffing rotas), whereas a leader sets a vision and inspires others to follow it (e.g. persuading teachers to adopt a new reading programme). The head teacher must do both: run the school day smoothly and inspire staff and parents.
parts.working: 1 mark (knowledge): leader = sets direction/inspires; manager = plans, organises, controls; up to 2 marks (application/explanation): difference applied to the school, e.g. drawing up timetables and budgets versus inspiring teachers to raise reading standards.

stem: Dr Kiran owns a dental clinic in Hyderabad with 4 dentists and 6 dental assistants. When deciding whether to open in the evenings, she held a staff meeting, listened to everyone's views and then took a vote. The senior dental assistant, who has worked there for 15 years, is respected by the other assistants, who often follow her advice. Last month the clinic's X-ray machine broke down and Dr Kiran had to rearrange 40 patient appointments.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify the leadership style Dr Kiran uses when deciding the clinic's opening hours.
parts.answer: Democratic leadership.
parts.working: 1 mark: democratic (accept participative/consultative). Do not accept laissez-faire.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain the term 'informal leader'.
parts.answer: A person with no formal position of authority who influences the attitudes and behaviour of a group because of personality, experience or popularity, e.g. the senior dental assistant whom other assistants follow.
parts.working: 1 mark (knowledge): person who influences others without a formal management role; up to 2 marks (application/explanation): why they have influence (experience, respect, personality) and/or an example from the clinic.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain one way Dr Kiran could use the senior dental assistant's informal leadership when the new evening opening hours are introduced.
parts.answer: Dr Kiran could ask the senior dental assistant to explain the evening rota to the other assistants and to help plan the first weeks. Because the other assistants often follow her advice, they are more likely to accept the change and volunteer for evening shifts, so the new hours start smoothly.
parts.working: 1 mark (knowledge): an informal leader influences colleagues without formal authority; up to 2 marks (application/explanation): the senior assistant's respect is used to win acceptance of the change (e.g. volunteers for evening shifts, smoother start).

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define the term 'paternalistic leadership'.
parts.answer: A style in which the leader makes decisions on behalf of employees but does so in what they believe is the employees' best interests, looking after their welfare like a parent.
parts.working: 1 mark: leader makes the decisions (may consult but decides); 1 mark: decisions are taken in the interests/welfare of employees.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one reason why a paternalistic leadership style might suit a family-owned bakery in Gujranwala.
parts.answer: Many staff have worked for the family for years and value security; the owner looking after their welfare (e.g. paying for medical bills, flexible leave at Eid) builds loyalty, so labour turnover stays low and experienced bakers are kept.
parts.working: 1 mark (knowledge): feature of paternalistic leadership (care for staff welfare, leader decides); up to 2 marks (application/explanation): linked to the bakery, e.g. loyal long-serving bakers, small family business, effect on turnover/loyalty.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Analyse one advantage to a construction company building a motorway in Balochistan of having informal leaders among its site workers.
parts.answer: Informal leaders, such as an experienced foreman respected by the labourers, can pass on and explain management instructions in the workers' own language; workers accept changes (e.g. new safety rules) more readily because they trust him; fewer disputes and faster adoption of safe working mean fewer accidents and delays, keeping the project on schedule and avoiding penalty clauses.
parts.working: Indicative content: informal leaders improve communication; win acceptance of change; reduce conflict; raise morale. Marks: Knowledge 1, Application 1, Analysis 3. Analysis Level 2 (2–3): a developed chain of cause and effect linked to a remote motorway site with large work gangs and deadlines; Level 1 (1): a simple statement of effect. Only one point is required; no credit for evaluation.

stem: Al Noor Stadium in Doha seats 45,000 people and hosts football matches, concerts and exhibitions. It employs 120 permanent staff and up to 400 temporary staff on event days. Last year two events lost money because security and catering costs were higher than budgeted. Omar has just been appointed general manager.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Analyse two of Fayol's functions of management that Omar must carry out as the new general manager of Al Noor Stadium.
parts.answer: Planning: Omar must set objectives (e.g. host 30 events a year) and plan staffing and security for each match; without plans, crowd safety and revenue targets would be at risk. Controlling: he must compare actual results (ticket sales, costs per event) with targets and take corrective action, e.g. cutting overtime if security costs exceed budget, which protects the stadium's profit. (Also accept organising, commanding, coordinating.)
parts.working: Indicative content: planning (objectives, event calendar, staffing); organising (allocating staff and resources, structure); commanding (giving instructions, motivating 400 match-day staff); coordinating (ticketing, security and catering working together); controlling (measuring performance against targets, corrective action). Marks: Knowledge 2, Application 2, Analysis 4. Analysis Level 2 (3–4): two developed chains of cause and effect applied to a stadium hosting football matches and concerts in Doha; Level 1 (1–2): undeveloped or generic chains. Exactly two points are credited; no credit for evaluation.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Hilal Insurance (an invented company) has a regional claims office in Faisalabad with 70 claims handlers. The previous manager checked every claim personally and believed staff would avoid work if not watched closely. Average claim approval took 19 days and labour turnover was 18 %. The new manager, Mehwish, believes most employees want responsibility and can be trusted to use their own judgement.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Analyse two ways in which Mehwish's view of employees, using McGregor's Theory X and Theory Y, could influence the leadership style at the regional office.
parts.answer: Mehwish holds Theory Y views (staff enjoy work, seek responsibility). She is therefore likely to delegate authority and use a democratic style, e.g. letting claims handlers settle claims up to a limit, which speeds up decisions and improves customer satisfaction. Her predecessor held Theory X views (staff dislike work, need control), leading to an autocratic style with close supervision and checking of every claim; this slowed processing and demotivated staff, which may explain the 18 % turnover. Moving to Theory Y could raise motivation, but only if staff are trained to handle responsibility.
parts.working: Indicative content: Theory X → autocratic, close supervision, few delegated decisions, tight control; Theory Y → delegation, democratic/participative style, job enrichment, trust; effects on motivation, speed of decisions, turnover. Marks: Knowledge 2, Application 2, Analysis 4. Analysis Level 2 (3–4): two developed chains of cause and effect applied to the insurance claims office and its data (approval time, turnover); Level 1 (1–2): undeveloped or generic chains. Exactly two points are credited; no credit for evaluation.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Rangoon Organics was started in Myanmar by Thura, who made every decision himself when it had 15 employees. It now has 260 employees and offices in Myanmar, Thailand and Singapore. Thura still approves all purchases above US$500 and all new customer contracts. Two experienced country managers resigned last year, saying they had 'no freedom to manage'.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Analyse two reasons why the autocratic leadership style used by the founder may be less effective now that Rangoon Organics has grown.
parts.answer: With 260 staff in three countries, the founder cannot make every decision quickly: decisions bottleneck at the top, so country managers cannot respond to local supermarket buyers, losing orders. Experienced country managers are given no authority, so they become demotivated and may leave (two left last year), raising recruitment costs and losing market knowledge. (Also accept: lack of new ideas from staff; poor communication over long distances.)
parts.working: Indicative content: decision bottleneck/slower responses as the business grows; demotivation of skilled managers; loss of ideas/innovation; communication problems across countries. Marks: Knowledge 2, Application 2, Analysis 4. Analysis Level 2 (3–4): two developed chains of cause and effect applied to an organic food exporter that has grown from 15 to 260 staff in three countries; Level 1 (1–2): undeveloped or generic chains. Exactly two points are credited; no credit for evaluation.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate whether laissez-faire leadership is the most suitable style for the head of a university research laboratory developing new vaccines in Karachi.
parts.answer: Laissez-faire suits highly qualified, self-motivated scientists: freedom encourages creativity and new research ideas, and Theory Y staff may resent close control. However, vaccine research is tightly regulated: safety, ethics approvals and grant deadlines need clear direction and control, so a purely hands-off approach risks breaches and missed deadlines. Judgement: a mainly laissez-faire style for research design, combined with firm (more autocratic) control over safety and compliance, is likely best; the most suitable style depends on the task and the experience of each team member (contingency approach).
parts.working: Indicative content: advantages of laissez-faire for expert, motivated researchers (creativity, motivation, ownership); risks: lack of coordination, missed deadlines, safety/regulatory failures, junior researchers lacking guidance; alternatives such as democratic or situational leadership. Evaluation: depends on staff experience, nature of tasks (creative vs compliance), regulation, funding deadlines; a supported conclusion, e.g. a mixed or contingency style is most suitable. Marks: Knowledge 2, Application 2, Analysis 2, Evaluation 6. Evaluation Level 3 (5–6): judgements weighed throughout and a supported conclusion specific to the business; Level 2 (3–4): a judgement with some support in context; Level 1 (1–2): an unsupported or generic judgement.

stem: Margalla Cement (an invented company) employs 1,100 people at two plants. In 2023 it made a loss of Rs 2.1 billion. Faisal was appointed CEO and used an autocratic style: he cut costs, closed a kiln and approved every purchase himself. In 2025 the business made a profit of Rs 1.4 billion. However, absenteeism rose from 3 % to 7 % and two experienced plant managers resigned. The board now wants to start exporting cement to East Africa, which will need quick decisions by managers based in Mombasa.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate whether Faisal should change his leadership style to improve the performance of Margalla Cement.
parts.answer: Arguments for changing: an autocratic style may have suited the crisis (fast cost cutting) but data show falling morale – absenteeism has risen from 3 % to 7 % and two plant managers resigned – and the move into export markets needs ideas and quick local decisions, which a more democratic style with delegation would support. Arguments against: cement plants are safety-critical and capital-intensive, so central control over costs and safety may still be needed; profits have recovered under the current style; a sudden change may confuse staff. Judgement: Faisal should adapt rather than abandon his style – keep firm control over safety and capital spending but delegate decisions on export sales and plant improvements to managers, as the business is no longer in crisis.
parts.working: Indicative content: evidence of success (return to profit) versus warning signs (absenteeism up, resignations, need for innovation for exports); features of autocratic vs democratic/delegation; situational leadership – the right style depends on circumstances that have changed. Evaluation: whether the crisis is over; skills of managers; risks of change; a decision specific to Margalla Cement. Marks: Knowledge 2, Application 2, Analysis 2, Evaluation 6. Evaluation Level 3 (5–6): judgements weighed throughout and a supported conclusion specific to the business; Level 2 (3–4): a judgement with some support in context; Level 1 (1–2): an unsupported or generic judgement.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
Karakoram Couriers (an invented company) delivers parcels across northern Pakistan.
Timeline:
2015: Founded by Rashid Khan, who treats staff 'like family', pays for staff weddings and medical costs and makes all decisions himself.
2020: 1,400 employees, 22 depots. Revenue Rs 6.2 billion.
2024: Staff threaten a strike when a new rota is introduced without consultation; the rota is withdrawn.
2025: Rashid retires. Sana Javed, a former logistics manager at a multinational, becomes CEO.
2026 plan: introduce app-based parcel tracking, automate route planning for 30 % of routes and merge 22 depots into 15.
Appendix 1: Revenue growth fell from 11 % (2022) to 2 % (2025).
Appendix 2: Staff survey 2025 – 81 % say they are loyal to the business; 34 % trust senior management to manage change fairly.
Appendix 3: A national rival has cut prices by 12 % and offers next-day delivery to all 22 towns Karakoram serves.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Advise Sana Javed on the leadership approach she should use at Karakoram Couriers over the next three years.
parts.answer: Options: continue the founder's paternalistic style; adopt a democratic/participative style; use a more autocratic style to drive the technology change; or a situational mix. Analysis: the 2026 plan (app-based tracking, 30 % of routes automated, merger of depots) is a major change that staff fear (Appendix 2 survey: only 34 % trust senior management); a purely autocratic style would speed implementation but could trigger the resistance seen in the 2024 strike threat; involving depot managers and informal leaders in planning (democratic) would win acceptance and use local knowledge but is slower when a rival is cutting prices (Appendix 3). Recommendation: a situational approach – consult and involve staff on how the change is implemented (depot teams, regular briefings), delegate route decisions to depot managers, but set clear non-negotiable deadlines and targets herself; keep paternalistic elements (job security pledge, retraining) that staff value. Success depends on her emotional intelligence and on communication.
parts.working: Indicative content: features of leadership styles; timeline evidence that the founder's paternalistic style built loyalty but slowed decisions; scale and urgency of change; staff trust data; competitor pressure; role of emotional intelligence and informal leaders. Evaluation: a clear recommendation that matches the style to the stage of change and the evidence, with conditions (e.g. depends on depot managers' ability, speed needed to respond to the rival). Marks: Knowledge 3, Application 3, Analysis 6, Evaluation 8. Analysis needs three or four developed chains using the timeline and appendices. Evaluation Level 3 (6–8): a clear, justified decision that weighs the evidence and is specific to the business and the time period; Level 2 (3–5): a judgement with partial support; Level 1 (1–2): assertion only.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define the term 'off-the-job training'.
parts.answer: Training that takes place away from the employee's normal place of work/workstation, e.g. at a college, training centre or online course provider.
parts.working: 1 mark: training away from the normal workplace/job; 1 mark: example or method, e.g. college course, external training centre, conference.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one advantage to a bank in Dubai of using a specialist recruitment agency to recruit IT security specialists.
parts.answer: IT security specialists are scarce; an agency already has a database of qualified candidates and can screen them for technical skills, so the bank fills vacancies faster and with suitable people, reducing the risk of cyber attacks while posts are empty.
parts.working: 1 mark (knowledge): agency has expertise/contacts/screens applicants, saving management time; up to 2 marks (application/explanation): applied to scarce IT security skills in a bank, e.g. speed of filling vital posts.

stem: RoshanPak installs rooftop solar panels in Lahore. It needs 25 more technicians. It spent Rs 180,000 on social media adverts. All 64 applicants took a practical wiring test costing Rs 3,500 per applicant. The best 30 were interviewed at a cost of Rs 2,000 per interview, and 25 were appointed.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify one stage of the recruitment and selection process used by RoshanPak.
parts.answer: Advertising the vacancy (also accept: shortlisting, practical skills test, interview).
parts.working: 1 mark for any one stage from the data.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain the term 'external recruitment'.
parts.answer: Filling a vacancy with someone from outside the business, e.g. RoshanPak advertising on social media to find technicians who do not already work for it; this brings in new skills but costs more and takes longer than internal recruitment.
parts.working: 1 mark (knowledge): appointing a person from outside the organisation; up to 2 marks (application/explanation): method (adverts, agencies) and/or a consequence, ideally applied to RoshanPak.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the recruitment and selection cost per technician appointed.
parts.answer: Rs 18,560 per technician.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define the term 'unfair dismissal'.
parts.answer: Ending an employee's contract for a reason that the law does not accept as valid, or without following a fair procedure, e.g. dismissing a worker for joining a trade union.
parts.working: 1 mark: termination of employment by the employer; 1 mark: for an unlawful/invalid reason or without a fair procedure (accept a valid example).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one reason why an air navigation service might use psychometric tests when selecting trainee air traffic controllers.
parts.answer: Psychometric tests measure aptitude and personality traits such as spatial reasoning, concentration and coping with stress; air traffic control is safety-critical, so the tests help screen out applicants who could not handle pressure, reducing the risk of errors and wasted training costs.
parts.working: 1 mark (knowledge): psychometric tests assess personality/aptitude/ability; up to 2 marks (application/explanation): linked to the stress and safety needs of air traffic control and to reducing training failures.

stem: SwiftDrop, a courier company in Karachi, sent all 40 of its van drivers on a two-day off-the-job defensive-driving course. The course fee was Rs 22,000 per driver. Each driver normally generates Rs 4,500 of contribution per day, which was lost while they were on the course. Accident repair costs fell from Rs 310,000 per month before the course to Rs 155,000 per month after it.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the payback period, in months, of the defensive-driving course.
parts.answer: 8 months.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one reason why the fall in accident repair costs might not be caused only by the training.
parts.answer: Other factors may have changed at the same time, e.g. the company replaced old vans, the city opened new roads, or the period after training was the dry season with fewer accidents in rain; so the saving may be overstated.
parts.working: 1 mark (knowledge): other variables can affect accident rates; up to 2 marks (application/explanation): specific factor applied to a courier fleet and its effect on the estimate.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Shifa Medical Centre (an invented hospital) in Islamabad is opening a new cardiac wing and has recruited 120 nurses from the Philippines and Kenya. When it last recruited overseas nurses, without an induction programme, 25 % left within a year and two serious medication errors were linked to staff who did not understand the hospital's procedures.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Analyse two benefits to Shifa Medical Centre of providing a structured induction programme for the nurses recruited from overseas.
parts.answer: The nurses need to learn local procedures, hospital IT systems and some Urdu phrases; a two-week induction means they reach full productivity faster, so the new wing can open on time and fewer agency nurses are needed. Induction also helps them settle socially (housing support, mentors), so they feel valued and are less likely to leave in the first year – important because turnover among overseas recruits was 25 % last time, and each replacement costs recruitment fees and visa costs.
parts.working: Indicative content: faster productivity/fewer errors (patient safety); understanding of policies, procedures and culture; feeling valued → lower early labour turnover; legal and safety compliance; builds teamwork with existing staff. Marks: Knowledge 2, Application 2, Analysis 4. Analysis Level 2 (3–4): two developed chains of cause and effect applied to a hospital recruiting 120 overseas nurses for a new wing; Level 1 (1–2): undeveloped or generic chains. Exactly two points are credited; no credit for evaluation.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Analyse one disadvantage to a university of appointing an internal candidate as the new head of its computer science department.
parts.answer: An internal candidate brings no new ideas from other universities or industry; the department may keep teaching outdated programming courses, so graduate employability and student applications fall, damaging the university's reputation and fee income. (Also accept: a vacancy is created elsewhere; resentment from unsuccessful colleagues.)
parts.working: Indicative content: limited pool of talent; lack of fresh ideas; resentment among colleagues; creates another vacancy. Marks: Knowledge 1, Application 1, Analysis 3. Analysis Level 2 (2–3): a developed chain of cause and effect linked to a university computer science department in a fast-changing subject; Level 1 (1): a simple statement of effect. Only one point is required; no credit for evaluation.

stem: Crescent Auto Parts makes brake parts in Karachi for car assemblers. Demand has fallen because car sales have dropped by 40 %. It will make 200 of its 650 production workers redundant. The average length of service of the 200 workers is 9 years and their average weekly pay is Rs 9,500. The company has agreed with the union to pay 2 weeks' pay for each year of service.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the total redundancy payments Crescent Auto Parts must make.
parts.working: Payment per worker = 9 years × 2 weeks × Rs 9,500 = Rs 171,000 (M1 M1); × 200 workers (M1) = Rs 34,200,000 (A1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Analyse two costs, other than redundancy payments, that Crescent Auto Parts may face as a result of the redundancies.
parts.answer: Lower morale among the 450 remaining workers ('survivor syndrome') may reduce productivity and raise absenteeism, increasing unit costs. Loss of experienced workers' skills means the business may need to retrain remaining staff on the old lines or pay recruitment costs if demand recovers. (Also accept: damage to reputation/employer brand; risk of industrial action and lost output.)
parts.working: Indicative content: survivor syndrome/lower morale and productivity; loss of skills and knowledge; future recruitment and training costs; industrial action; reputational damage with community/customers. Marks: Knowledge 2, Application 2, Analysis 4. Analysis Level 2 (3–4): two developed chains of cause and effect applied to a car-parts factory cutting 200 of its 650 jobs; Level 1 (1–2): undeveloped or generic chains. Exactly two points are credited; no credit for evaluation.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate whether training is the most important factor in improving customer service at a chain of 30 mobile phone repair shops.
parts.answer: Training gives technicians the skills to repair quickly and correctly and teaches counter staff how to handle complaints, directly improving service. However, other factors matter: recruitment and selection of staff with the right attitude; motivation and pay (well-trained but poorly paid staff may leave, wasting training); having parts in stock and good systems for booking repairs; leadership and checks on quality. Judgement: training is necessary but not sufficient – for a repair chain, the quality of technical skills is central so training is probably the most important single factor, provided it is supported by good selection and retention; otherwise training spending is lost through turnover.
parts.working: Indicative content: role of training (on-the-job, off-the-job) in skills and customer handling; alternative factors: selection, motivation, pay, inventory of parts, processes, leadership, quality systems. Evaluation: weighing factors for a repair business, link between training and turnover, a supported conclusion. Marks: Knowledge 2, Application 2, Analysis 2, Evaluation 6. Evaluation Level 3 (5–6): judgements weighed throughout and a supported conclusion specific to the business; Level 2 (3–4): a judgement with some support in context; Level 1 (1–2): an unsupported or generic judgement.

stem:
OneCloud (an invented company) is a software company in Lahore with 180 engineers. It has won a contract to manage cloud services for a Gulf bank, starting in 6 months, and needs 40 more engineers.
Option 1: recruit experienced engineers from abroad. Average pay Rs 1.2 million per month each; relocation cost Rs 2.5 million each; most would sign 2-year contracts.
Option 2: recruit local graduates and train them on a 9-month programme. Average pay Rs 350,000 per month each; training cost Rs 1.8 million each.
Labour turnover at OneCloud is 22 % a year; a staff survey says graduates trained by the company are more loyal.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate whether OneCloud should recruit experienced engineers from abroad rather than train local graduates to fill its 40 vacancies.
parts.answer: Recruiting from abroad: engineers are productive at once (needed for the contract starting in 6 months), bring cloud-security experience the firm lacks; but cost is high (salary Rs 1.2 million a month vs Rs 350,000, plus relocation), they may leave when contracts end, and visas take time. Training graduates: much cheaper per engineer even after a 9-month programme, builds loyalty and lowers turnover, supports reputation as an employer; but too slow for the new contract and the first cohort may lack experience. Judgement: a mix – hire a small number of experienced engineers (e.g. 8–10) to meet the contract deadline and lead teams, while training graduates for the rest; this balances speed against cost, depending on the bank client's deadline and OneCloud's cash position.
parts.working: Indicative content: speed and skills of external experienced recruits vs cost, retention, cultural fit; training graduates: lower cost, loyalty, long-term skills, but time and risk; contract deadline; cash flow. Evaluation: conclusion using the case data and the time constraint; recommend a balanced approach or one option with clear conditions. Marks: Knowledge 2, Application 2, Analysis 2, Evaluation 6. Evaluation Level 3 (5–6): judgements weighed throughout and a supported conclusion specific to the business; Level 2 (3–4): a judgement with some support in context; Level 1 (1–2): an unsupported or generic judgement.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Roots & Wings (an invented business) runs 12 private schools in Rawalpindi and Islamabad. It selects teachers using a 30-minute interview with the principal. Last year it appointed 50 teachers; after one term, 15 were rated 'unsatisfactory' by inspectors and 9 left within the year. Parents have complained about the quality of teaching in mathematics.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate whether interviews are the best method of selecting teachers for the Roots & Wings School group.
parts.answer: Interviews allow the panel to judge communication, subject knowledge and attitude, and the candidate can ask questions. But interviews are poor predictors of classroom performance, can be biased (e.g. favouring confident speakers), and the school group's data show 30 % of teachers appointed last year were rated 'unsatisfactory' after one term. Alternatives: a demonstration lesson observed by senior staff, subject tests, references, assessment of lesson plans. Judgement: interviews are useful but not best on their own; a demonstration lesson plus a structured interview gives better evidence of teaching ability, although it costs more time – justified because poor appointments affect students' results and the group's reputation.
parts.working: Indicative content: strengths and weaknesses of interviews; alternative/complementary selection methods (demonstration lesson, tests, references, assessment centre); cost of a poor appointment; context data. Evaluation: a supported judgement for the school group, e.g. interviews combined with a teaching demonstration. Marks: Knowledge 2, Application 2, Analysis 2, Evaluation 6. Evaluation Level 3 (5–6): judgements weighed throughout and a supported conclusion specific to the business; Level 2 (3–4): a judgement with some support in context; Level 1 (1–2): an unsupported or generic judgement.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Thal Dairies processes milk into yoghurt and butter. In 2024 it had an average of 320 employees and 48 employees left. In 2025 it had an average of 350 employees and 77 employees left.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the labour turnover at Thal Dairies for 2024 and for 2025.
parts.working: Labour turnover = leavers ÷ average number of employees × 100 (M1). 2024: 48 ÷ 320 × 100 = 15.0 % (A1). 2025: 77 ÷ 350 × 100 = 22.0 % (M1 A1).

author: HomiLabs

stem: The Snow Peak Hotel in Gilgit employs 85 staff. Each employee is expected to work 280 days a year. Last year 1,428 working days were lost through absence, mostly during the busy summer season.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the absenteeism rate at the Snow Peak Hotel last year.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain the term 'labour turnover'.
parts.answer: The percentage of a business's employees who leave during a period (usually a year), measured as leavers ÷ average number of employees × 100; at the hotel, seasonal staff leaving after summer would raise it.
parts.working: 1 mark (knowledge): proportion/percentage of workforce leaving in a period (formula accepted); up to 2 marks (application/explanation): explanation of meaning or causes/effects, ideally applied to the hotel.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain one way the Snow Peak Hotel could reduce absenteeism.
parts.answer: Introduce a return-to-work interview and an attendance bonus paid at the end of the season; staff know absence is monitored and have a financial reason to attend, so fewer days are lost in the busy months.
parts.working: 1 mark (knowledge): valid method (attendance bonus, return-to-work interviews, better welfare/working conditions, flexible rotas); up to 2 marks (application/explanation): how it works and why it suits a hotel with seasonal peaks.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define the term 'labour productivity'.
parts.answer: Output per employee (or per worker-hour) in a given time period, calculated as total output ÷ number of employees.
parts.working: 1 mark: output per worker/per hour; 1 mark: over a stated period / formula total output ÷ number of employees.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one reason why a workforce plan for a sports-goods manufacturer in Sialkot might turn out to be inaccurate.
parts.answer: The plan depends on a forecast of demand; if a large overseas order for footballs ahead of a World Cup is won or lost unexpectedly, the number of stitchers needed will be very different from the plan.
parts.working: 1 mark (knowledge): plan based on forecasts of demand/labour supply/turnover that may be wrong; up to 2 marks (application/explanation): applied to an export-dependent sports-goods maker with changing orders or new technology.

stem: Golden Crust Bakery in Lahore employs 12 full-time bakers and 8 part-time bakers. Each part-time baker works half the hours of a full-time baker. Last month the bakery produced 46,800 loaves.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate labour productivity at Golden Crust Bakery in loaves per full-time equivalent (FTE) employee per month.
parts.answer: 2,925 loaves per FTE per month.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one limitation of using labour productivity to judge the performance of the bakery's workers.
parts.answer: It measures quantity not quality: bakers could raise loaves per worker by rushing, giving more burnt or misshaped loaves that are wasted; also output may rise because of a new oven rather than worker effort.
parts.working: 1 mark (knowledge): productivity ignores quality / affected by capital equipment / demand; up to 2 marks (application/explanation): applied to the bakery.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Kohinoor Ceramics makes floor tiles. Before introducing a new production layout, its monthly wage bill was Rs 7,200,000 and it produced 48,000 boxes of tiles a month. After the new layout was introduced, workers received a 10 % pay rise and output rose to 57,600 boxes a month with the same number of workers.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the labour cost per unit before and after the new production layout was introduced.
parts.answer: Before: Rs 150 per unit; after: Rs 137.50 per unit.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one reason why Kohinoor Ceramics' profit might not rise even though labour cost per unit has fallen.
parts.answer: Labour is only one cost: if the new layout needed a large loan, interest and depreciation may rise; or prices may fall if extra output can only be sold at a discount, so profit may not increase.
parts.working: 1 mark (knowledge): other costs/revenue may change; up to 2 marks (application/explanation): applied, e.g. extra output must be sold, raw material and energy costs, investment costs.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Bright Future (an invented business) runs 15 private schools in Islamabad with 400 teachers. Labour turnover among teachers was 28 % last year, compared with an average of 12 % for private schools in the city. Many teachers leave for better-paid jobs in the Gulf.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Analyse two effects of the high labour turnover on the Bright Future school group.
parts.answer: Recruitment and induction costs rise: with 28 % of 400 teachers leaving each year, about 112 must be replaced, each costing advertising, interviews and training, which reduces funds available for facilities. Continuity of teaching suffers: students have new teachers mid-year, so exam results fall and parents move children to rival schools, cutting fee income. (Also accept: lower morale of remaining staff, loss of experience.)
parts.working: Indicative content: higher recruitment, selection and training costs; disruption to learning and results; damage to reputation/fee income; workload and morale of remaining staff; loss of experienced teachers. Marks: Knowledge 2, Application 2, Analysis 4. Analysis Level 2 (3–4): two developed chains of cause and effect applied to a school group with 28 % teacher turnover; Level 1 (1–2): undeveloped or generic chains. Exactly two points are credited; no credit for evaluation.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Mercy General Hospital employs 400 nurses. Labour turnover among nurses (resignations and transfers, not retirements) is expected to be 12 % next year, and a further 15 nurses will retire. A new wing opening next year will need 60 additional nurses.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the number of nurses Mercy General Hospital must recruit during the next year.
parts.answer: 123 nurses.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Analyse two factors, other than labour turnover, that the hospital should consider when preparing its workforce plan.
parts.answer: Availability of qualified nurses in the labour market: if many nurses are emigrating, it may need to recruit abroad or offer higher pay, so the plan must allow more time and budget. Changes in technology and services: if the new wing uses remote patient monitoring, fewer nurses may be needed per bed but they need new skills, so the plan must include training. (Also accept: demand forecasts/patient numbers, legal staffing ratios, budget, retirements age profile, flexible contracts.)
parts.working: Indicative content: forecast patient demand; legal nurse-to-patient ratios; skills and training needs; labour market supply/migration; budget constraints; technology; age profile. Marks: Knowledge 2, Application 2, Analysis 4. Analysis Level 2 (3–4): two developed chains of cause and effect applied to a hospital opening a 60-nurse wing; Level 1 (1–2): undeveloped or generic chains. Exactly two points are credited; no credit for evaluation.

author: HomiLabs

stem: PixelForge (an invented company) develops mobile games in Lahore and employs 150 staff. It has signed contracts for three new games over the next two years. HR data: labour turnover among junior developers is 35 %; absenteeism in the customer support team is 9 %; output per developer (lines of tested code per month) rose 8 % last year after new software tools were introduced.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Analyse two ways in which PixelForge could use labour data to improve its workforce planning.
parts.answer: Absenteeism data by team show that the support team loses 9 % of days, so planners can build in extra cover or investigate causes before a product launch, avoiding missed deadlines. Labour turnover data show 35 % of junior developers leave within 18 months; the plan can therefore include more graduate recruits each year and retention measures, so the business has enough developers for the projects it has won.
parts.working: Indicative content: productivity data to estimate staff needed for future output; turnover to forecast replacement needs; absenteeism to plan cover; trends by department to target action. Marks: Knowledge 2, Application 2, Analysis 4. Analysis Level 2 (3–4): two developed chains of cause and effect applied to a games developer planning staffing for projects; Level 1 (1–2): undeveloped or generic chains. Exactly two points are credited; no credit for evaluation.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
Orient Motors (an invented company) assembles vehicles at two plants.
Plant A: 1,260 workers; output 151,200 vehicles per year; absenteeism 3.1 %; spare capacity 25,000 vehicles per year; makes established petrol models.
Plant B: 840 workers; output 92,400 vehicles per year; absenteeism 6.4 %; makes a new electric model launched last year; located next to the port used for exports.
The board is considering closing Plant B to cut costs.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate labour productivity (vehicles per worker per year) at Plant A and Plant B.
parts.answer: Plant A: 120 vehicles per worker; Plant B: 110 vehicles per worker.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Evaluate whether Orient Motors should close Plant B to improve its performance.
parts.answer: For closing: Plant B's productivity is 8.3 % lower (110 vs 120), its absenteeism is double (6.4 % vs 3.1 %), and Plant A has spare capacity of 25,000 vehicles – not enough for all of B's 92,400 vehicles, so closure needs extra capacity or a fall in output. Against: B makes the new electric model, its productivity gap could be due to the new model's start-up, not worker effort; closure means redundancy costs, loss of skills and conflict with the union and local community; B is close to the port. Judgement: closing Plant B is not justified on productivity data alone; better to investigate causes of absenteeism and improve B (training, soft HRM), and review again in a year; closure only if the gap persists and demand falls.
parts.working: Indicative content: interpretation of productivity and absenteeism data; capacity constraint; causes of differences (product mix, new model, age of equipment, management); costs of closure (redundancy, reputation, union); alternatives. Evaluation: judgement using the data, limits of labour data, and a conditional recommendation. Marks: Knowledge 2, Application 2, Analysis 2, Evaluation 6. Evaluation Level 3 (5–6): judgements weighed throughout and a supported conclusion specific to the business; Level 2 (3–4): a judgement with some support in context; Level 1 (1–2): an unsupported or generic judgement.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Valley Treks employs 8 permanent staff and hires up to 35 temporary guides, drivers and cooks in summer. Bookings fell by 60 % in one year because of floods that closed roads, then rose by 80 % the following year.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate whether workforce planning is worthwhile for Valley Treks, a small tour operator in Swat.
parts.answer: For: demand is highly seasonal (June–August), so planning how many guides, drivers and cooks to hire, and when, avoids paying idle staff in winter and being short in summer; planning training for certified guides ensures safety. Against: the business is small (8 permanent staff) and demand is unpredictable (weather, security, road closures, exchange rates for foreign tourists), so detailed plans may quickly become out of date and cost management time. Judgement: a simple, flexible workforce plan (core permanent staff plus a list of trusted seasonal workers on temporary contracts) is worthwhile; a detailed long-term plan is not.
parts.working: Indicative content: purpose of workforce planning; seasonal labour needs; flexible contracts; costs of planning for a small firm; uncertainty of forecasts. Evaluation: a supported conclusion for a small seasonal business, e.g. a simple flexible plan is worthwhile. Marks: Knowledge 2, Application 2, Analysis 2, Evaluation 6. Evaluation Level 3 (5–6): judgements weighed throughout and a supported conclusion specific to the business; Level 2 (3–4): a judgement with some support in context; Level 1 (1–2): an unsupported or generic judgement.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
Zest Foods (an invented company) makes snacks in Karachi.
Timeline:
2021: New factory opened; 550 employees.
2023: Twelve-hour night shifts introduced to raise output.
2024: A rival snack maker opens a factory 3 km away, paying 15 % higher wages.
2025: Operating profit margin falls from 11 % to 7 %.
Appendix 1: Average employees and leavers: 2023 – 600 employees, 108 leavers; 2024 – 650 employees, 156 leavers; 2025 – 700 employees, 217 leavers. Estimated cost of replacing each leaver: Rs 250,000.
Appendix 2: Exit interviews 2025 – pay 42 %; shift patterns 33 %; poor supervision 15 %; other 10 %.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Advise the board of Zest Foods on the most suitable strategy to reduce labour turnover over the next three years.
parts.answer: Calculations from Appendix 1: turnover 2023 = 108 ÷ 600 = 18 %, 2024 = 156 ÷ 650 = 24 %, 2025 = 217 ÷ 700 = 31 %; cost in 2025 = 217 × Rs 250,000 = Rs 54.25 million. Exit interviews show pay (42 %) and shift patterns (33 %) are the main reasons. Options: a pay rise for line workers (direct response to main cause but adds to costs when margins are falling); flexible shifts and better welfare (addresses 33 % and is cheaper); improved induction and career paths; soft HRM approach. Recommendation: combine a targeted pay increase for production staff, funded partly by the saving from lower turnover (e.g. halving turnover saves about Rs 27 million a year), with flexible rota choices, and monitor turnover quarterly; success depends on the competitor's pay levels and the business's cash flow.
parts.working: Indicative content: calculate/interpret turnover trend and cost; causes from exit interviews; options (pay, flexible shifts, welfare, training, career progression, soft HRM); trade-off with falling margins; competitor pay. Evaluation: a justified recommendation of a combination with priorities, conditions and monitoring. Marks: Knowledge 3, Application 3, Analysis 6, Evaluation 8. Analysis needs three or four developed chains using the timeline and appendices. Evaluation Level 3 (6–8): a clear, justified decision that weighs the evidence and is specific to the business and the time period; Level 2 (3–5): a judgement with partial support; Level 1 (1–2): assertion only.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define the term 'hard HRM'.
parts.answer: An approach that treats employees as a resource to be used as efficiently as possible, like other inputs, with a focus on cost control, short-term contracts and close monitoring of performance.
parts.working: 1 mark: employees treated as a resource/cost to be minimised or used efficiently; 1 mark: features, e.g. top-down control, short-term contracts, little consultation.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one benefit to an accountancy firm in Karachi of offering flexi-time to its staff.
parts.answer: Staff can choose start and finish times around core hours, so those with childcare or long commutes are less stressed; the firm keeps experienced accountants who might otherwise leave, especially valuable before the tax-return deadline when skilled staff are hardest to replace.
parts.working: 1 mark (knowledge): flexi-time = choice of working hours around core time; benefit (retention, motivation, wider recruitment pool, longer opening hours); up to 2 marks (application/explanation): applied to accountants, e.g. busy tax season, Karachi traffic.

stem: ParcelHub runs a large warehouse near Dubai that packs online orders. It employs 90 permanent staff and 300 order pickers on zero-hours contracts. The number of hours offered to pickers each week varies with online sales, which are highest during the Ramadan and year-end sales.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify one type of flexible employment contract, other than a zero-hours contract.
parts.answer: Part-time contract (also accept temporary/fixed-term contract, job share, flexi-time, home working).
parts.working: 1 mark for any valid type.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain the term 'zero-hours contract'.
parts.answer: An employment contract in which the employer does not guarantee any minimum hours; the worker is called in when needed and paid only for hours worked – e.g. ParcelHub pickers called in during sales peaks.
parts.working: 1 mark (knowledge): no guaranteed minimum hours / paid only for hours worked; up to 2 marks (application/explanation): explanation of use (called when needed, flexibility for employer) applied to the warehouse.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain one disadvantage to ParcelHub's workers of being employed on zero-hours contracts.
parts.answer: Their income is uncertain: in quiet weeks they may get only a few hours, so they cannot plan for rent and bills, which causes stress and may lead them to look for permanent jobs elsewhere.
parts.working: 1 mark (knowledge): uncertain hours/income, lack of security or benefits; up to 2 marks (application/explanation): applied to warehouse pickers and the consequence.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define the term 'management by objectives (MBO)'.
parts.answer: A method of managing performance in which managers and employees agree specific objectives for each employee that are linked to the organisation's objectives, and performance is then reviewed against them.
parts.working: 1 mark: objectives agreed between manager and employee; 1 mark: linked to departmental/corporate objectives and used to review performance.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one way a hospital laboratory could measure the performance of its technicians.
parts.answer: Average turnaround time from sample arrival to result, compared with a target (e.g. 4 hours for blood tests); faster times mean doctors can treat patients sooner. (Also accept error/re-test rate, tests per technician per shift.)
parts.working: 1 mark (knowledge): a valid performance measure; up to 2 marks (application/explanation): how it is used and why it matters in a laboratory.

stem: Saqib & Co is an engineering design firm in Islamabad. It will allow 60 staff to work from home 3 days a week. This means it can give up one floor of its office, saving rent of Rs 450,000 per month. It will pay each of the 60 home workers an internet and electricity allowance of Rs 5,000 per month.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the net annual saving to Saqib & Co from introducing home working.
parts.answer: Rs 1,800,000 per year.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one way home working might reduce the performance of Saqib & Co's staff.
parts.answer: Less face-to-face contact makes it harder for junior engineers to ask questions and learn from senior staff, so mistakes in designs take longer to spot and projects may be delayed.
parts.working: 1 mark (knowledge): reduced communication/supervision/teamwork, distractions, isolation; up to 2 marks (application/explanation): applied to an engineering design firm.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
Amanat Health Insurance (an invented company) has two claims teams. Last month:
Team X: 12 employees, 5,760 claims processed, 144 claims contained errors.
Team Y: 9 employees, 4,860 claims processed, 73 claims contained errors.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate claims processed per employee per month and the error rate for Team X and Team Y.
parts.answer: Team X: 480 claims per employee, error rate 2.50 %. Team Y: 540 claims per employee, error rate 1.50 %.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one reason why these two measures may not give a full picture of each team's performance.
parts.answer: The teams may handle different types of claim: if Team X deals with complex hospital claims and Team Y with simple pharmacy claims, X will naturally process fewer and make more errors; customer satisfaction and speed are also not measured.
parts.working: 1 mark (knowledge): measures ignore complexity/quality/customer satisfaction/other factors; up to 2 marks (application/explanation): applied to the two teams.

author: HomiLabs

stem: The Palm Crest Hotel in Dubai is a five-star hotel with 520 employees from 30 countries. Labour turnover is 40 % a year. Online reviews often praise the building but criticise 'unfriendly' and 'inconsistent' service. The new HR director wants to change from a hard to a soft HRM approach.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Analyse two benefits to the Palm Crest Hotel of adopting a soft HRM approach.
parts.answer: Investing in training and career paths for front-line staff increases their skills and commitment, so they deliver the personalised service that luxury guests expect, leading to better online reviews and higher room rates. Consulting staff and treating them as valued assets increases motivation and reduces labour turnover (currently 40 %), cutting recruitment costs and keeping staff who know regular guests' preferences.
parts.working: Indicative content: soft HRM: employees as valuable assets, training, consultation, empowerment, long-term development; effects: motivation, customer service quality, lower turnover, flexibility/ideas. Marks: Knowledge 2, Application 2, Analysis 4. Analysis Level 2 (3–4): two developed chains of cause and effect applied to a five-star hotel with high turnover and reputation-sensitive customers; Level 1 (1–2): undeveloped or generic chains. Exactly two points are credited; no credit for evaluation.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Analyse one disadvantage to a university of introducing 360-degree appraisal for its lecturers.
parts.answer: Students and colleagues may give biased feedback – e.g. students rating strict markers poorly – so lecturers may lower assessment standards to get better ratings, reducing academic quality and the value of the university's degrees. (Also accept: time-consuming to collect and analyse; may cause conflict between colleagues.)
parts.working: Indicative content: bias/unreliable feedback; time and cost; conflict/anxiety among staff. Marks: Knowledge 1, Application 1, Analysis 3. Analysis Level 2 (2–3): a developed chain of cause and effect linked to lecturers being rated by students, colleagues and managers; Level 1 (1): a simple statement of effect. Only one point is required; no credit for evaluation.

stem: Hashoo Electronics (an invented company) assembles air conditioners and fans in Lahore. Demand in May–July is three times demand in November–January. It employs 300 permanent staff and up to 500 temporary assembly workers, and contracts out its IT support and security.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Analyse two benefits to Hashoo Electronics of organising its workforce into a core of permanent staff and a periphery of temporary and contract workers.
parts.answer: Flexibility: the business can increase the number of periphery assembly workers for the Eid and summer air-conditioner season and release them afterwards, so labour costs match demand and it does not pay idle staff in winter. Retention of key skills: core staff (designers, quality engineers) receive permanent contracts and training, so the expertise needed for new inverter models stays in the business, protecting quality and innovation.
parts.working: Indicative content: numerical flexibility, lower average labour costs, matching labour to seasonal demand, ability to buy specialist skills when needed, focus of training and motivation on core staff. Marks: Knowledge 2, Application 2, Analysis 4. Analysis Level 2 (3–4): two developed chains of cause and effect applied to a seasonal electronics manufacturer; Level 1 (1–2): undeveloped or generic chains. Exactly two points are credited; no credit for evaluation.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate whether a hard HRM approach is the most appropriate for a fast-food chain with 60 restaurants.
parts.answer: For hard HRM: tasks are standardised and low-skilled, labour is a large share of costs, demand varies by hour so flexible part-time/zero-hours staff reduce costs; close monitoring ensures consistent speed and hygiene. Against: very high turnover raises recruitment and training costs; poorly motivated staff give poor service, harming the brand; managers and kitchen supervisors need development. Judgement: a mixed approach – hard elements for flexible scheduling and standard procedures, soft elements (training, recognition, promotion of crew to managers) to reduce turnover; the balance depends on the chain's positioning (budget vs premium) and the local labour market.
parts.working: Indicative content: features of hard and soft HRM; standardised tasks; labour cost; turnover; customer service; brand consistency. Evaluation: a contingent conclusion; justify a balance for a fast-food chain. Marks: Knowledge 2, Application 2, Analysis 2, Evaluation 6. Evaluation Level 3 (5–6): judgements weighed throughout and a supported conclusion specific to the business; Level 2 (3–4): a judgement with some support in context; Level 1 (1–2): an unsupported or generic judgement.

stem:
Insight Analytics (an invented company) is a market-research firm in Karachi with 220 staff. Twelve months ago it introduced hybrid working (2 days in the office, 3 days at home).
Before hybrid: average reports completed per analyst per month 31; absenteeism 4.2 %; new products developed per year 5.
After hybrid: reports per analyst per month 34; absenteeism 2.6 %; new products developed 2.
Staff survey: 78 % want hybrid working to continue. Client complaints about slow replies rose from 12 to 29 per quarter. Graduates hired in the last year say they 'learn slowly' at home.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate whether Insight Analytics should make hybrid working permanent for all employees.
parts.answer: Evidence for: reports per analyst rose from 31 to 34 per month (+9.7 %); absenteeism fell from 4.2 % to 2.6 %; office costs fell; staff survey shows 78 % prefer hybrid, so it aids retention and recruitment from other cities. Evidence against: client complaints about slow responses rose; new graduates report weaker learning; team innovation (new products) fell from 5 to 2; data security risks. Judgement: make hybrid permanent for experienced staff but require new graduates to be office-based for their first year and set core in-office days for team projects; review client satisfaction quarterly.
parts.working: Indicative content: productivity, absenteeism, cost and retention data; disadvantages for training, communication, innovation, client service; different needs of different staff groups. Evaluation: conclusion based on the data, possibly a modified policy. Marks: Knowledge 2, Application 2, Analysis 2, Evaluation 6. Evaluation Level 3 (5–6): judgements weighed throughout and a supported conclusion specific to the business; Level 2 (3–4): a judgement with some support in context; Level 1 (1–2): an unsupported or generic judgement.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Crescent Model Schools (an invented business) has 9 schools and 320 teachers in Peshawar. Results in mathematics have fallen for three years. There is no formal system for reviewing teachers' work. The owners plan to introduce annual appraisal by each school principal, with a pay bonus for teachers rated 'excellent'.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate whether introducing annual performance appraisal will improve the performance of teachers at Crescent Model Schools.
parts.answer: Appraisal sets targets, identifies training needs and recognises good teachers, which can raise motivation and results, especially if linked to classroom observation and mentoring. However, it may be seen as a box-ticking exercise, causing stress and conflict if linked to pay; principals need training to appraise fairly; teaching quality is hard to measure, and focusing on exam results may narrow teaching. Judgement: appraisal will improve performance only if it is developmental (training, feedback, peer observation) rather than judgemental, and if the school follows up with resources; otherwise it may have little effect.
parts.working: Indicative content: purposes of appraisal; links to motivation theory; methods (self, peer, 360, observation); problems (bias, time, stress, measurement); link to pay. Evaluation: conditional judgement for the schools. Marks: Knowledge 2, Application 2, Analysis 2, Evaluation 6. Evaluation Level 3 (5–6): judgements weighed throughout and a supported conclusion specific to the business; Level 2 (3–4): a judgement with some support in context; Level 1 (1–2): an unsupported or generic judgement.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define the term 'employee welfare'.
parts.answer: The care a business provides for the physical and mental wellbeing of its employees beyond basic pay, e.g. health care, safe conditions, counselling, canteens or transport.
parts.working: 1 mark: looking after the wellbeing/health/comfort of employees; 1 mark: beyond pay, with a valid example.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one way a construction company could improve the welfare of its site workers during the summer heat in Multan.
parts.answer: Change shift times so that heavy work is done from 5 am to 11 am and stopped in the hottest afternoon hours, with shaded rest areas and free drinking water; this reduces heatstroke and absence and keeps workers productive.
parts.working: 1 mark (knowledge): a valid welfare measure; up to 2 marks (application/explanation): applied to extreme heat on a building site and its effect.

stem: Meridian Pharma (an invented company) employs 1,800 staff in Karachi. Average hourly pay for men is Rs 1,250 and for women is Rs 1,050. Most women work in quality-control laboratories, while most senior research posts are held by men.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the gender pay gap at Meridian Pharma as a percentage of men's average hourly pay.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain the term 'equality policy'.
parts.answer: A written statement setting out how a business will ensure that all employees and applicants are treated fairly and given the same opportunities, whatever their gender, religion, ethnicity, disability or age – e.g. Meridian publishing pay bands and using mixed interview panels.
parts.working: 1 mark (knowledge): policy/commitment to treat people fairly with equal opportunities; up to 2 marks (application/explanation): how it operates (recruitment, pay, promotion) applied to Meridian.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain one benefit to Meridian Pharma of reducing its gender pay gap.
parts.answer: Women scientists are more likely to stay and to apply, widening the talent pool for its research laboratories and reducing recruitment costs; it also helps win contracts from international partners who check suppliers' equality records.
parts.working: 1 mark (knowledge): benefit: recruitment/retention, motivation, reputation, contracts; up to 2 marks (application/explanation): applied to a pharmaceutical company.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two forms of discrimination that could occur when a business recruits staff.
parts.answer: Any two of: rejecting applicants because of gender; religion; ethnicity/caste; disability; age; marital status.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two valid forms (grounds) of discrimination.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one benefit to an international airline of employing cabin crew from many different nationalities.
parts.answer: Crew who speak passengers' languages and understand their customs (e.g. Arabic, Mandarin, Urdu speakers on the relevant routes) can communicate safety information and give better service, increasing customer satisfaction and repeat bookings.
parts.working: 1 mark (knowledge): benefit of diversity (languages, cultural understanding, wider talent pool); up to 2 marks (application/explanation): applied to passengers on international routes.

stem: Sapphire Knitwear (an invented company) employs 900 workers, of whom 360 are women. It has opened a crèche (childcare centre) for workers' children, which costs Rs 360,000 per month to run. Before the crèche, labour turnover among women machinists was 30 %.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify one welfare benefit, other than the crèche, that Sapphire Knitwear could provide.
parts.answer: Subsidised transport to work (also accept: health clinic, subsidised meals, counselling, housing).
parts.working: 1 mark for any valid welfare benefit.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the annual cost of the crèche per female employee.
parts.answer: Rs 12,000 per female employee per year.
parts.working: Annual cost = 360,000 × 12 = Rs 4,320,000 (M1); ÷ 360 female employees (M1) = Rs 12,000 (A1).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain one way the crèche could benefit Sapphire Knitwear.
parts.answer: Mothers no longer have to leave to care for young children, so labour turnover among skilled machinists falls; the firm saves recruitment and training costs and keeps output and quality high.
parts.working: 1 mark (knowledge): benefit: retention, attendance, recruitment, motivation, reputation with buyers; up to 2 marks (application/explanation): applied to a knitwear factory with many women workers.

author: HomiLabs

stem: CodeCraft (an invented company) is a software house in Lahore with 260 engineers, of whom 9 % are women. About 40 % of the computer-science graduates who apply to CodeCraft are women. CodeCraft plans to offer remote working, a women's mentoring scheme and safe late-night transport. Two of its European clients ask suppliers to report on workforce diversity.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Analyse two benefits to CodeCraft of its plan to recruit more women software engineers.
parts.answer: Wider talent pool: in a market short of engineers, recruiting from the 40 % of computer-science graduate applicants who are women lets CodeCraft fill vacancies faster, so projects are delivered on time. Better products and contracts: mixed teams bring different perspectives, leading to apps that suit a wider range of users, and foreign clients that require supplier diversity reports are more likely to award contracts, increasing revenue.
parts.working: Indicative content: wider pool of applicants/skills shortage; diverse ideas/creativity; better understanding of customers; reputation and client requirements; retention through inclusive culture. Marks: Knowledge 2, Application 2, Analysis 4. Analysis Level 2 (3–4): two developed chains of cause and effect applied to a software house where 9 % of engineers are women; Level 1 (1–2): undeveloped or generic chains. Exactly two points are credited; no credit for evaluation.

author: HomiLabs

stem: GlobalMart (an invented company) is a supermarket multinational with stores in 14 countries in Asia, the Middle East and Africa. Head office wants every country to adopt one policy, including targets for women managers and a ban on asking candidates' age or marital status.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Analyse two problems that GlobalMart might face when introducing the same diversity and equality policy in all 14 countries in which it operates.
parts.answer: Different laws and cultures: some countries have different employment laws or social attitudes to, for example, women working night shifts; a single policy may break local laws or be resisted by staff, causing conflict and legal costs. Implementation and monitoring costs: managers in each country need training and data systems to track recruitment and promotion, which is expensive and may be done unevenly, so the policy has little real effect and damages credibility.
parts.working: Indicative content: legal differences; cultural/religious norms; resistance from local managers; cost of training and monitoring; difficulty measuring outcomes; risk of being seen as imposing head-office values. Marks: Knowledge 2, Application 2, Analysis 4. Analysis Level 2 (3–4): two developed chains of cause and effect applied to a multinational retailer in 14 countries; Level 1 (1–2): undeveloped or generic chains. Exactly two points are credited; no credit for evaluation.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Analyse one way an employee wellbeing programme, offering free counselling and gym membership, could improve productivity at a commercial bank.
parts.answer: Bank staff face long hours and pressure from sales targets; counselling helps them manage stress, reducing burnout and sickness absence; with fewer days lost and more focused staff, each employee handles more customers and makes fewer errors, raising output per employee.
parts.working: Indicative content: lower stress/absence; better health/energy; motivation (feeling valued); lower turnover. Marks: Knowledge 1, Application 1, Analysis 3. Analysis Level 2 (2–3): a developed chain of cause and effect linked to bank staff under pressure; Level 1 (1): a simple statement of effect. Only one point is required; no credit for evaluation.

stem: Sunrise Textiles set an objective in 2022 that 20 % of its managers would be women by 2025. In 2023 it had 160 managers, of whom 14 were women. In 2025 it had 180 managers, of whom 27 were women.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage of managers at Sunrise Textiles who were women in 2023 and in 2025.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain whether the data show that Sunrise Textiles has achieved its equality objective.
parts.answer: The share of women managers rose by 6.25 percentage points, but the target was 20 % by 2025, so the objective was not achieved; progress may also reflect new junior management posts rather than equal promotion.
parts.working: 1 mark (knowledge): compare 15 % with the 20 % target; up to 2 marks (application/explanation): comment on progress or on what the data do not show.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate whether spending on employee welfare is worthwhile for a low-cost airline.
parts.answer: Low-cost airlines compete on price, so extra costs (staff health care, rest facilities, counselling) may raise fares and reduce competitiveness. However, pilots and cabin crew work under fatigue and safety pressure; welfare reduces sickness absence (which can cancel flights), improves retention of scarce pilots and engineers, and protects safety and reputation. Judgement: targeted welfare that reduces absence, fatigue and turnover is worthwhile because a cancelled flight or a safety incident costs far more; spending that does not affect safety or retention should be limited.
parts.working: Indicative content: cost pressures and price competition; welfare benefits: absence, retention of scarce skills, safety, reputation, legal requirements; measurement of returns. Evaluation: judgement balancing cost and benefits for a low-cost airline. Marks: Knowledge 2, Application 2, Analysis 2, Evaluation 6. Evaluation Level 3 (5–6): judgements weighed throughout and a supported conclusion specific to the business; Level 2 (3–4): a judgement with some support in context; Level 1 (1–2): an unsupported or generic judgement.

stem: Indus Tech Bank (an invented bank) has 6,000 employees. 46 % of graduate trainees are women, but only 18 % of middle managers and 7 % of senior managers are women. Exit interviews show women leave mainly because of long hours and lack of childcare. The central bank has asked banks to increase the number of women customers and employees.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate whether the board of Indus Tech Bank should introduce a target that 30 % of its senior managers will be women by 2030.
parts.answer: For: currently 7 % of senior managers are women but 46 % of graduate entrants are, so talent is being lost; diverse leadership may improve decisions and serve the growing number of women customers; the central bank encourages gender-inclusive banking. Against: targets may be seen as unfair by men, causing resentment, or lead to promotion before candidates are ready; the target does not tackle causes (lack of flexible work, transport, childcare). Judgement: introduce the target but support it with mentoring, flexible working and fair promotion criteria, monitored annually; without these the target is unlikely to be met and may cause conflict.
parts.working: Indicative content: data on pipeline of women; benefits of diversity; regulatory/reputation pressure; risks of targets (tokenism, resentment); root causes and supporting policies. Evaluation: a conditional judgement for the bank. Marks: Knowledge 2, Application 2, Analysis 2, Evaluation 6. Evaluation Level 3 (5–6): judgements weighed throughout and a supported conclusion specific to the business; Level 2 (3–4): a judgement with some support in context; Level 1 (1–2): an unsupported or generic judgement.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
Rehmat Healthcare (an invented company) runs 5 private hospitals in Lahore.
Timeline:
2021: 1,500 nurses; labour turnover 14 %.
2023: Many nurses leave to work in the Gulf; turnover rises to 22 %.
2025: Turnover 26 %; two wards closed for 3 months because of staff shortages.
2026: Board considers a staff welfare programme: staff hostel, safe night transport, childcare and mental-health support. Cost Rs 600 million over 3 years.
Appendix 1: Spending on agency nurses rose from Rs 90 million (2021) to Rs 420 million (2025).
Appendix 2: Exit interviews 2025 – unsafe/expensive night travel 35 %; burnout 28 %; pay 25 %; other 12 %.
Appendix 3: A 20 % pay rise for all nurses would cost Rs 300 million per year.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Advise the board of Rehmat Healthcare whether to invest in a staff welfare programme to solve its nurse shortage.
parts.answer: Option 1: welfare programme (staff hostel, transport, childcare, mental-health support; cost Rs 600 million over 3 years). Benefits: addresses the main reasons for leaving in Appendix 2 (night travel 35 %, burnout 28 %); turnover cut from 26 % could reduce agency nurse spending of Rs 420 million a year (Appendix 1); better patient care and reputation. Risks: does not match Gulf salaries (pay 25 %); payback depends on how far turnover falls. Option 2: pay rise of 20 % (cost Rs 300 million a year, every year). Recommendation: invest in welfare as the core strategy, because it targets the largest causes and costs less over time than a permanent pay rise, combined with a smaller retention bonus for nurses who stay 3 years; monitor turnover and agency spend each quarter.
parts.working: Indicative content: use of appendices (turnover, agency costs, reasons for leaving); options compared on cost and effect; link to motivation theory (Herzberg hygiene factors); risks; timescale. Evaluation: a justified decision with conditions and monitoring. Marks: Knowledge 3, Application 3, Analysis 6, Evaluation 8. Analysis needs three or four developed chains using the timeline and appendices. Evaluation Level 3 (6–8): a clear, justified decision that weighs the evidence and is specific to the business and the time period; Level 2 (3–5): a judgement with partial support; Level 1 (1–2): assertion only.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define the term 'span of control'.
parts.answer: The number of subordinates who report directly to one manager or supervisor.
parts.working: 1 mark: number of subordinates/employees; 1 mark: directly responsible to one manager.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one disadvantage of a wide span of control for a ward sister supervising 25 nurses in a hospital.
parts.answer: She has too little time to supervise and support each nurse; mistakes in medication or patient care may go unnoticed and new nurses receive little guidance, which risks patient safety.
parts.working: 1 mark (knowledge): wide span → less supervision/communication/support; up to 2 marks (application/explanation): applied to nursing and patient safety.

stem: QuickBite (an invented company) runs 120 fast-food restaurants in Pakistan. The CEO is supported by 3 regional directors. Each regional director manages area managers, who each look after 8 restaurant managers. Each restaurant manager supervises a crew. All menu, pricing and supplier decisions are taken at head office.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the number of levels of hierarchy at QuickBite.
parts.answer: 5 levels.
parts.working: 1 mark: 5 (CEO, regional directors, area managers, restaurant managers, crew).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain the term 'chain of command'.
parts.answer: The route by which instructions pass down, and information passes up, through the levels of hierarchy; at QuickBite a new menu instruction passes from the CEO through regional directors and area managers to restaurant managers and crew.
parts.working: 1 mark (knowledge): line of authority/path of instructions from top to bottom of the hierarchy; up to 2 marks (application/explanation): applied to QuickBite's levels.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain one advantage to QuickBite of centralised decision-making.
parts.answer: Head office decides menus, prices and suppliers, so every restaurant offers the same products and quality; customers get a consistent brand experience, and bulk buying lowers costs.
parts.working: 1 mark (knowledge): centralisation = decisions taken at the top; up to 2 marks (application/explanation): advantage (consistency, control, economies of bulk buying) applied to a fast-food chain.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define the term 'decentralisation'.
parts.answer: Passing decision-making authority from head office/senior management to managers lower down the hierarchy or in different locations.
parts.working: 1 mark: decision-making authority moved away from the centre/top; 1 mark: to lower levels or local/branch managers.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one difference between line authority and staff authority, using an example from a cement company.
parts.answer: A line manager (e.g. the plant manager) has direct authority to give instructions to subordinates in the chain of command; a staff specialist (e.g. the environmental adviser) gives advice to line managers but cannot instruct production workers.
parts.working: 1 mark (knowledge): line = direct authority over subordinates; staff = advisory/specialist role; up to 2 marks (application/explanation): examples from a cement company.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define the term 'matrix structure'.
parts.answer: An organisational structure in which employees report to two managers: a functional/department manager and a project (or product) manager, with teams drawn from different departments.
parts.working: 1 mark: staff from different functions grouped into project teams; 1 mark: dual reporting – functional manager and project manager.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one advantage for a food manufacturer of organising its structure by product division (e.g. dairy, snacks, beverages).
parts.answer: Each division's managers focus on the needs of one market, e.g. the beverages division can respond quickly to summer demand and competitors' new drinks; performance of each division is easy to measure.
parts.working: 1 mark (knowledge): product structure groups activities by product; up to 2 marks (application/explanation): advantage applied to the food manufacturer's divisions.

stem: HomeStyle (an invented furniture retailer) has a CEO, 4 regional managers each paid Rs 900,000 per month, and 32 store managers (8 per region). It plans to remove the regional manager layer. The 32 store managers will instead report to 2 new area directors, each paid Rs 1,300,000 per month.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the span of control of each area director after the change.
parts.answer: 16 store managers.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the annual saving in management salaries from the change.
parts.answer: Rs 12,000,000 per year.
parts.working: Old cost 4 × 900,000 = Rs 3,600,000 per month; new cost 2 × 1,300,000 = Rs 2,600,000 per month (M1); monthly saving Rs 1,000,000 (M1); × 12 = Rs 12,000,000 (A1).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain one risk to HomeStyle of the change.
parts.answer: With a span of 16, area directors cannot visit each store often; problems such as poor displays or staff disputes may be missed, and store managers may feel unsupported, reducing sales.
parts.working: 1 mark (knowledge): delayering risk: wider span, overload, loss of experienced managers, morale; up to 2 marks (application/explanation): applied to the stores.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Kisan Bank (an invented bank) has 300 branches across rural Pakistan. All loans above Rs 200,000 are approved at head office in Islamabad, which takes on average 21 days. Farmers often need finance quickly before the sowing season, and microfinance companies approve loans in 3 days.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Analyse two benefits to Kisan Bank of decentralising lending decisions to its branch managers.
